body:
Problem

When one task reads several input partitions (for example, a storage-partitioned join on a subset of the partition keys), Spark 4.1 opens a reader per partition and hands the previous reader's metrics to the next one through initMetricsValues.
BatchDataReader, RowDataReader and MergingSortedRowDataReader inherit the no-op default, so numSplits, numDeletes and scanDuration only count the last reader in each task. Raised by @manuzhang in #17562 (comment).

Fix

The three readers now override initMetricsValues and add the inherited values to their own.
MergingSortedRowDataReader now reports scanDuration too, summed across its file readers.
Spark 4.2 isn't affected: it no longer groups input partitions inside DataSourceRDD and doesn't call initMetricsValues, so this change is 4.1 only.
Spark 4.0 has the same bug (the new test fails there with numSplits 2 instead of 5). I'll backport once this merges.

Testing

New TestSparkReadMetrics case runs a subset-key SPJ that puts 5 partitions into 2 tasks, with a merge-on-read delete in each partition. Without the fix, numSplits and numDeletes are 2 instead of 5, on both the vectorized and row paths.
New TestMergingSortedRowDataReader case covers the merging reader, including inherited scanDuration, and fails the same way without the fix.
TestSparkReadMetrics, TestMergingSortedRowDataReader pass. spotlessCheck and checkstyle pass.
title: Spark 4.1: Keep read metrics from earlier readers in the same task

body:
Bumps datamodel-code-generator from 0.85.0 to 0.86.0.

Release notes
Sourced from datamodel-code-generator's releases.

0.86.0
Breaking Changes
Code Generation Changes

Base64 bytes with length constraints now use EncodedBytes - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary, a format: byte string with minLength or maxLength used to generate conbytes(...), which did not decode base64. With --field-constraints it used to generate Base64Bytes with a Field(max_length=...). It now generates Annotated[bytes, Field(max_length=8), EncodedBytes(encoder=Base64Encoder)], which decodes the base64 text and checks the lengths on the encoded text, as JSON Schema counts them. Field values are now the decoded bytes instead of the raw text. Under --field-constraints, inputs whose base64 text is longer than the limit are now rejected, even when the decoded bytes fit. Generated modules now import Annotated, Field, EncodedBytes and Base64Encoder. Pydantic checks these lengths on the text only from 2.10 on, and an explicit --target-pydantic-version 2 now warns about each such field (#4798)
Strict bytes no longer skip base64 decoding for mapped byte strings - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary and --strict-types bytes, format: byte fields used to generate StrictBytes, or conbytes(..., strict=True) when they had lengths, and held the raw text. They now generate Base64Bytes, or the EncodedBytes form when they have lengths, and decode the base64 text, so validated values change. FastAPI path, query, header and cookie parameters with this combination no longer stop generation with an error (#4798)
Mapped byte formats now decode base64 when mapped without constraints - With --type-mappings string+byte=binary, code paths that map a type and format without constraints now pass base64 decoding through. For example, a format: byte string member of a multi-type type list now generates Base64Bytes, as in Base64Bytes | list[int], instead of plain bytes. Its runtime value becomes the decoded bytes (#4798)

Other Output Changes
These change generated output compared with 0.85.0, but only where 0.85.0 output failed or for options that are new in this release.

Integer and subclass enums that list null no longer get a None member - An enum with a value type base (the IntEnum written for type: integer, or a --use-subclass-enum class such as (int, Enum)) that lists null used to get a member such as integer_None = None, which made the generated module raise TypeError at import. That member is no longer generated, and an enum whose only value is null becomes a RootModel[None]. Class names and field defaults are unchanged (#4884, #4889)
Discriminator tags keep no pattern their values already satisfy - Pydantic discriminator tag fields written with Field() constraints no longer carry a pattern that every tag value satisfies. Such output failed at import in 0.85.0 because the tag was no longer a usable discriminator. Tags whose values contradict their own pattern are unchanged (#4888)
Optional one-value Literal discriminator tags default to their value - A tag such as kind: Literal['card'] | None = None is now written as kind: Literal['card'] = 'card'. The discriminated union failed at import before; a standalone model using such a tag now defaults to and dumps 'card' instead of None (#4895)
The builtin formatter wraps long Annotated[...] = None assignments like black - Where 0.85.0 put the None default in parentheses on its own lines, the line is now split inside the annotation, as black does. The code is equivalent, but --check runs with a dated preset (which uses the builtin formatter) report the reformatting (#4794)
Refinements of options new in this release - --use-tag-as-union-variant-name no longer repeats the key in prefixed names of models inside key-named branches (#4903), and --use-single-value-enum-as-const types nullable single-value unions as Literal[...] | None keeps mixed-type single-value branches apart instead of merging them into one Enum (#4926, #4927), […]

Release notes
Sourced from mkdocs-material's releases.

mkdocs-material-9.8.0

[!WARNING]
Material for MkDocs reaches end of life on May 5, 2027. Critical fixes and security updates continue until that date.
We're continuing our work with Zensical, a maintained successor built by the team behind Material for MkDocs. It carries forward what we've learned from building documentation tools with this community, with Markdown authoring, a familiar design, and full control over your content. Zensical is Open Source and MIT-licensed.
You can evaluate Zensical alongside MkDocs using your existing mkdocs.yml. Check plugin compatibility and compare your pages, navigation, search, and customizations before switching. The classic theme variant preserves the appearance of Material for MkDocs. See the migration guide for the steps and current compatibility details.
Upcoming changes on November 5

This is primarily a security release. It raises dependency minimums to address known vulnerabilities. We recommend upgrading to this release and updating your dependency lockfiles.
Python 3.11 or newer is now required. Python 3.8–3.10 are no longer supported.

Updated Node build-time dependencies to fix vulnerabilities
Updated Python dependency minimums and required Python 3.11
Removed RSS from recommended dependencies
Updated project status and maintenance links
Updated CLI notice with end-of-life and migration guidance
Removed redirects from recommended dependencies

Previous dependency ranges allowed versions with known vulnerabilities. The new minimums cover core Python dependencies and the optional git and imaging extras, including GitPython 3.2.1 or newer for the git extra.
Recent releases of mkdocs-rss-plugin and mkdocs-redirects depend on ProperDocs, a separate static site generator that Material for MkDocs does not require. Removing these plugins from the recommended extra keeps its dependency footprint smaller and leaves the choice of additional tools to each project. If your project uses RSS feeds or redirects, declare the relevant plugin explicitly in your own dependencies.
The CLI notice now gives the May 5, 2027 end-of-life date and links to the Zensical migration guide. It also clarifies that third-party ProperDocs migration notices do not represent a recommendation from the Material for MkDocs team. Package metadata now marks the project as inactive and includes maintenance and migration links.

Error Prone 2.51.0
New checks:

HashCodeInObjectsHash: Detect redundant hashCode() or Objects.hash() calls inside Objects.hash(...), and simplify single-argument Objects.hash(x) calls to Objects.hashCode(x).
LoopToTestParameter: Suggest migrating loops in unit tests to TestParameterInjector.
MissingJavadoc: Flag public types that are missing Javadoc comments (disabled by default).
PreferCharsetOverload: Prefer calling method and constructor overloads that accept a Charset over those that accept a String encoding name.
PreferPreconditions: Suggest using Guava's Preconditions instead of explicit if-throw statements for parameter validation (disabled by default).

body:
Closes #18737
Since #13631, BaseTransaction.expireSnapshots() goes through appendUpdate, which only wires deleteWith(enqueueDelete) for SnapshotUpdate. RemoveSnapshots implements ExpireSnapshots, so its delete callback stays null and the expired manifest lists, manifests and data files are removed by FileIO when the transaction-local commit() runs, before anything reaches the catalog. If the process dies or commitTransaction() fails, the table keeps referencing snapshots whose files are gone.
With this change the transaction gives ExpireSnapshots a delete callback too. The expired files go into a separate set, expiredFiles, and commitTransaction() deletes them only after the commit succeeds. If the commit fails they stay, and cleanUp() does not touch them. This is the deferred delete we had from #218 and #9183.
expiredFiles is cleared each time the updates are applied again on a refreshed base, so a retry only deletes what that attempt expired. It is a concurrent set because executeDeleteWith() runs the delete callback on the caller's executor. Note that this executor only runs the queueing now. The deletes themselves run after the commit, like before 1.10.
Two tests look at the state between the two commits, one with the default executor and one with a four thread delete executor. On main the files are already gone at that point. The existing transaction tests only look at the end state, so they did not catch this.
Two more tests came out of the review. One retries after another commit cherry-picks a staged snapshot that the first attempt expired. The other fails the commit and checks that the files are still there.
Happy to open the 1.10.x and 1.11.x backports once this is in.
title: Core: Defer file deletes of expireSnapshots inside a transaction until commit

JdbcTableOperations treats a zero-row result from the compare-and-swap UPDATE as a concurrent commit and throws CommitFailedException, which triggers cleanup of the files the commit wrote. When the database applied the UPDATE but the connection dropped before the response arrived, JdbcClientPool reconnects and replays the statement, which then matches zero rows: the catalog already points at the new metadata, and cleanup deletes the committed metadata file and manifests. With the default commit retries a concurrent writer can also silently rewind the table. On zero rows the operations now check the commit status strictly, as the Hive catalog does: success when the new location is current or in the history, CommitStateUnknownException when the check cannot run, CommitFailedException otherwise. JdbcViewOperations has the same pattern and is left for a follow-up.
Fixes #18743.
Test plan: with no commit retries, a replayed update (statement applied, zero rows reported) commits and the appended file is readable, which proves no cleanup ran; with default retries, a second writer that commits between the replayed update and the retry is not rewound, and both files stay visible; a zero-row update whose location never reached the catalog still fails with CommitFailedException and leaves no snapshot, which proves a real conflict is still refused. The first two tests fail on the current code.

body:
(Still evaluating the design, not ready for review yet)
Part of #18748
Flink upsert/CDC writers emit equality deletes only for the table's current partition spec, and an equality delete applies only to files of the same spec unless that spec is unpartitioned. After a spec change, updates and deletes therefore miss rows committed under older specs: upserts leave duplicate keys and deletes are lost. This affects v2 and v3 tables; the spec forbids equality deletes on v4, but Flink currently writes them there too, and this PR doesn't change that.
With this PR, when every partition spec of the table is partitioned only by equality fields (or has no partition fields), the writer also emits each equality delete for every older spec it saw at startup, provided the writer's key column types match the table's current schema. An older spec with no partition fields receives a global delete. A delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint stays a position delete. In all other cases the writer behaves as before. DeltaManifests keeps one delete manifest per spec (serializer version 3, still reads 1 and 2).
This fixes deletes against rows committed in earlier checkpoints. Not covered: tables with any spec partitioned on non-equality columns or containing void fields, writers whose key column types differ from the table's current schema, specs added after the writer started, dynamic-sink spec changes within one checkpoint, and cached dynamic-sink writer factories with stale spec metadata (related: #18675). Removing an older spec from table metadata (for example with cleanExpiredMetadata) while a writer runs fails its commits until the job is resubmitted, because the writer keeps targeting the specs it saw at startup; a failover reuses them.
Known costs: older specs receive deletes even when they no longer hold data, until they are removed from metadata and the job restarts; a global delete overlaps the per-spec deletes; tracked keys and open delete writers grow with the number of older specs.
Test plan:

TestDeltaTaskWriter: upsert after bucket(2) → bucket(4), and a CDC delete after adding bucketing, return the expected rows. Both fail on main. A CDC delete does not remove the same key from other partitions, a delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint keeps committed rows with the same key, and a writer schema older than the table's does not break writes.
TestIcebergFilesCommitter: an older-spec delete keeps its spec through the committer and applies (fails on main).
TestDynamicIcebergSink: an upsert in a later checkpoint, after the sink evolves the spec, leaves one row (two on main).
TestFlinkManifest: version 2 checkpoint state still restores.
All Flink 2.3 sink tests pass. Backports to 1.20 and 2.2 will follow.
title: [WIP] Flink: Fix silent duplicate keys and lost deletes after partition spec evolution

body:
Currently Iceberg Kafka Connector stalls when it receives bad records: a record that cannot be converted to the table schema fails the task in put(), and after every restart the task reads the same record and fails again. This PR implements support for bad record handling as per the configurations.
The user will be able to skip bad records instead of stalling, log the bad records if required and publish bad records to the DLQ topic.
The DLQ support is implemented using org.apache.kafka.connect.sink.ErrantRecordReporter provided by the Kafka Connect framework itself. The framework applies the following configurations, so the connector does not define them again:

errors.tolerance: 'none' (default) reports the record and fails the task; 'all' reports the record and skips it.
errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name: the DLQ topic for bad records.
errors.log.enable and errors.log.include.messages: log the bad records.

Without a DLQ or error logging the framework provides no reporter, and the task fails.
Only conversion failures are reported. File, catalog and schema update failures still fail the task, so a transient outage never sends good records to the DLQ. Offsets of reported records are committed with the next Iceberg commit only after their reports have completed.
This builds on #14618 by @devendra-nr (credited as co-author), rebased on the current main. It keeps the approach of reporting through ErrantRecordReporter, and in addition: relies on the framework's  own errors.* handling instead of redefining those configs, reports only conversion failures (so transient file or catalog errors can't send good records to the DLQ), waits for reports before offsets are committed, and adds docs.
Query engine
Kafka Connect
Closes #16876

Backports #17888 and #18453 to 1.11.x.
iceberg-bundled-guava 1.11.0 bundles Guava 33.6.0-jre, which is affected by CVE-2026-102554 (CVSS 4.0: 8.2). When Guava deserializes CompactHashMap, CompactHashSet or MapMakerInternalMap, it allocates an array sized by the serialized stream with no limit, so a crafted stream can cause an OutOfMemoryError. Add a dependency-free AuthManager that sets an Authorization: Bearer header on REST requests, as defined in RFC 6750.
The token is either read from a local file that is re-read periodically, or provided statically in the configuration. Obtaining and renewing the token is left to an external producer, such as a Kubernetes projected service account token or a sidecar.
The manager is selected with rest.auth.type=bearer. Tokens are validated against the RFC 6750 grammar, so that a malformed file cannot corrupt the Authorization header. If a reload fails, the last valid token is kept.

Add org.apache.iceberg.rest.auth.oauth2.OAuth2Manager, an AuthManager that authenticates against any OAuth2 authorization server with the client_credentials grant and renews access tokens before they expire by running the grant again. It is selected explicitly by class name (rest.auth.type=org.apache.iceberg.rest.auth.oauth2.OAuth2Manager) and configured with rest.auth.oauth2.* properties; the legacy oauth2 manager is unchanged.
Compared to the legacy manager, the new one discovers the token endpoint from the issuer URL (RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect Discovery), supports the client_secret_basic and client_secret_post authentication methods, and does not use token exchange for refresh.
Static tokens, token exchange and tokens vended by the catalog server in table responses are not supported. Session contexts carrying OAuth2 properties get a self-contained session; nothing is inherited from the catalog configuration.
The legacy properties credential, oauth2-server-uri, scope, audience and resource are translated with a warning, and the token endpoint falls back to the catalog's v1/oauth/tokens endpoint when neither a token endpoint nor an issuer URL is configured.
Important: the token property is not supported anymore by this manager, but is supported by the BearerAuthManager, see #18754. The suggested migration path for people using token is therefore to use the BearerAuthManager.
The implementation is built on the Nimbus OAuth SDK, and requests to the authorization server go through the catalog's RESTClient, which gains an unwrap(Class) method for that purpose.
Runtime bundle LICENSE files and dependency baselines are updated accordingly.
This PR supersedes #15703.
title: Core, REST: Add standards-based OAuth2Manager using the client credentials grant

body:
When a catalog returns more than one S3 credential, VendedCredentialsProvider rejects the refresh response with "only one S3 credential should exist", and long-running jobs fail when the first credentials expire. VendedAdlsCredentialProvider does the same for more than one ADLS credential per storage account. The REST spec allows more than one credential of the same type and says clients should choose the longest matching prefix.

S3: S3FileIO already builds one S3 client per credential prefix, but the refresh provider does not know which prefix its client serves. PrefixedS3Client now passes its storage prefix to the client factory in credentials.storage-prefix (next to the existing internal credentials.uri), and VendedCredentialsProvider uses the credential with the longest prefix that the storage prefix starts with. With a single credential, it behaves as before.
ADLS: ADLSFileIO keeps one SAS token per storage account and has no per-prefix clients, so there is no storage prefix to select by. VendedAdlsCredentialProvider now accepts several credentials for a storage account when they carry the same SAS token. Different tokens for one storage account are still rejected.

This follows #18716, which does the same for GCS. Nessie (projectnessie/nessie#13128 for GCS, projectnessie/nessie#13269 for S3 and ADLS) sends the same credential once for each of the table's locations, so its refresh responses contain more than one credential.
Test plan:

TestVendedCredentialsProvider: with more than one S3 credential and a storage prefix, the provider picks the longest prefix that covers the storage prefix and skips a longer one that does not cover it; the refresh fails when none covers it; one S3 credential is used even when its prefix does not cover the storage prefix. The existing test without a storage prefix still expects "only one S3 credential should exist".
TestS3FileIOCredentialRefresh.prefixedClientsRefreshWithTheirOwnCredential: S3FileIO with two storage credentials refreshes each prefix client with its own credential. Without the PrefixedS3Client change it fails with "only one S3 credential should exist".
TestVendedAdlsCredentialProvider.sameSasTokenForMultiplePrefixesOfStorageAccount: the same SAS token for two prefixes of one storage account is accepted. The existing test with different tokens still fails.
./gradlew :iceberg-aws:test :iceberg-azure:test for the classes above, and checkstyle and spotless for both modules.
Not tested against real S3 or ADLS.

Points for review:

credentials.storage-prefix is passed through the client factory properties, because AwsClientProperties creates the provider by reflection from those properties. The root client (prefix s3) also passes it; with several credentials, none of which covers s3, its refresh fails as before, but with a clearer message.
For ADLS I chose "same token" over "longest prefix", because a single token per storage account serves every path. Happy to change it if reviewers prefer another rule.

body:
When several clients create the same namespace at once, JdbcCatalog.createNamespace can let more than one of them pass its namespaceExists check. The first properties insert wins, and the others fail on the primary key of iceberg_namespace_properties. That SQLException comes out as UncheckedSQLException, which REST servers return as a 500, so the client can't tell that its create was simply rejected because the namespace already exists.
This catches the failed insert and checks again whether the namespace exists. If it does, createNamespace throws AlreadyExistsException, the same as when the first check finds it, and the REST layer returns 409. If the recheck succeeds and the namespace still doesn't exist, the original exception is rethrown, so other insert failures are reported as before. It doesn't depend on database-specific error codes. iceberg-go fixed the same race in its SQL catalog the same way (apache/iceberg-go#1635).
The new test, testCreateNamespaceLosingConcurrentCreate, is deterministic: it creates the namespace, then uses a spy so that the second create's first namespaceExists check returns false, as it would for a create that ran its check just before the winner's insert. Without the change it fails with UncheckedSQLException: Failed to execute: INSERT INTO iceberg_namespace_properties ...; with it, the create throws AlreadyExistsException and the winner's properties are unchanged.
Closes #18759.
Testing

./gradlew :iceberg-core:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.jdbc.TestJdbcCatalog on JDK 21: 157 tests, 0 failures, 12 skipped. The new test fails without the change.
./gradlew :iceberg-core:spotlessCheck passes.
End to end, with apache/iceberg-rest-fixture images built from this commit with and without the change (./gradlew :iceberg-open-api:shadowJar and the fixture Dockerfile): 6 clients creating the same namespace, 20 rounds, 4 runs each. Without the change, every round had one 200 and 18–57 of the 120 creates per run got a 500. With it, every round had one 200 and every other create got a 409, with no 500s.

Found by @aiskakov28 and @aldusialn.
title: Core: Throw AlreadyExistsException when a concurrent JDBC namespace create wins

ValueWriters.variants() returns a JVM-wide singleton whose metadata and value writers serialize through a reused buffer, so two threads writing Avro with variant columns could overwrite each other's bytes before they were encoded, silently writing another row's value or a corrupt one. This keeps that buffer in a thread-local, as UUIDWriter and DecimalWriter already do, so the shared instance is safe. Spark and Flink use their own variant writers and are not affected.

When s3.access-points.<bucket> is configured, S3FileIO.listPrefix builds each returned location from the access point instead of the bucket in the requested prefix. Listing s3://my-bucket/data/ returns s3://<access-point>/data/file for a file the table references as s3://my-bucket/data/file. Callers that match listed locations against table metadata, such as orphan file removal with prefix listing (the default in Flink DeleteOrphanFiles), then report every file as an authority mismatch, and ARN-based locations cannot be parsed back into the right bucket and key.

Under cooperative rebalancing, close(revoked) stops the worker, which discards the records buffered for every partition, including those that stay assigned, and seekToLastCommittedOffsets then rewinds only the partitions that have a committed offset. A kept partition that has never committed (a new connector, or a newly added topic or partition) keeps its position, so its discarded records are silently skipped. This remembers the first buffered offset of each partition and seeks a partition without a committed offset to it; partitions with a committed offset behave as before. The seek also no longer returns early when no assigned partition has committed.
Test plan: new TestKafkaUtils (with MockConsumer) and TestCommitterImpl#testCloseRewindsPartitionsWhoseBufferedRecordsWereDiscarded. body:
Why
Add a new v2 load endpoint so that clients can load format version 4 tables. This change is outlined in the REST spec PR for format version 4, #17642. Only the v2 endpoint can return a version 4 table, so clients that know only versions 1 to 3 never get one.
What changes
The Java REST client now uses the v2 endpoint to load and refresh a table when the server lists v2 in its configuration response. If the server does not list v2, the client uses v1 as before. Commits always use v1. Servers that do not know about v2 see no change, and the default list of endpoints in the client does not change.
If the server lists v2, the client does not need the v1 load endpoint. Refresh uses the same load path as the first load. RESTSessionCatalog sets this load path on the table operations after the newTableOps hooks return them. Subclasses that override these hooks keep working with no change. If a subclass makes the operations with its own table path, refresh continues to use that path.
CatalogHandlers.loadTable ( v1 load handler ): rejects a version 4 table with the new UnsupportedFormatVersionException, and the error message tells the user to use v2. This exception is a subclass of BadRequestException, so the server sends HTTP 400. CatalogHandlers.loadTableV2: returns tables at all format versions. A server that uses CatalogHandlers gets the v1 rule with no more changes. If such a server uses loadTable for version 4 tables now, it must use loadTableV2 for the v2 endpoint.
The Java client changes this error back to UnsupportedFormatVersionException, so code can find it without a check of the message. An old client that does not know the type gets BadRequestException with the same message.
The reference test server uses these two handlers and lists v2. A v1 load of a version 4 table gets HTTP 400.
Testing
New coverage

TestRESTCatalogV2LoadTable is a new suite. It checks that the client loads and refreshes tables with format versions 1 to 4 through v2, and that commits use v1.
The same suite checks that a client that uses only v1 gets UnsupportedFormatVersionException for a version 4 table.
It also checks a server that lists only v2 and a server that lists only v1. It checks that refresh uses the v2 path, and that operations with a custom path continue to refresh from that path. It also checks that a subclass that overrides the newTableOps hooks is still called and refreshes through v2.
TestCatalogHandlersLoadTable is a new suite. It checks that loadTable returns tables with format versions 1 to 3 and rejects version 4, and that loadTableV2 returns all versions.
TestErrorHandlers has new tests. They check that the client gets UnsupportedFormatVersionException for this error type, and BadRequestException for other HTTP 400 errors.
TestResourcePaths and TestEndpoint check the new path and the new endpoint.
The v2 tests fail if the client uses v1 instead of v2. The rejection tests fail if the server does not do the check.

Coverage from the current suites
The reference test server now lists v2, so the current REST suites use v2 for each load. These suites are TestRESTCatalog, TestFreshnessAwareLoading, TestReferencedByQueryParam, and the REST compatibility kit in open-api. TestRESTCatalog and TestFreshnessAwareLoading override the newTableOps hooks with the signatures from before this PR, and they pass with no change.

body:
This PR builds on #18782, and its first commit contains the changes from #18782. To review only the changes in this PR, use https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18783/changes/3c43da7bce1816a74a4a4a7828160dedbb40903d..a7fbb38d7287eac0fd4cfded6e7197df7829fd9e
Why
In format version 4, the location field in table metadata is optional. Paths in the metadata can also be relative to the table location. A client must know the table location to find these files and to write new files. The format spec says that the catalog must supply the location when the metadata does not include it. This change is outlined in the REST spec PR for format version 4, #17642. It adds a table-location field for this purpose to load, commit, and unregister responses.
What changes
The Java REST client reads table-location from load, commit, and unregister responses. If the field is present, the client uses it as the table location, instead of the location field in the metadata. The client does not send this location back to the server in later commits, so the catalog keeps control of the location. The client keeps the response as it was received, so the same response gives the same JSON again.
The client rejects a table-location that is not an absolute path with a URI scheme. It also rejects a version 4 response that has no location at all. Without this check, the error occurs later in a write, and the cause is hard to find.
The server code in CatalogHandlers sends table-location only for version 4 tables. Responses for versions 1 to 3 do not change.
One result can be unexpected. A create transaction can start from a staged response that gets its location from table-location. The create commit then sends that location to the server. This is necessary, because the create commit is the step that saves the location of the new table.
Testing
New coverage

TestLoadTableResponseParser and TestUnregisterTableResponseParser have new tests. They check JSON with and without table-location, and that table-location overrides location.
The same tests check that the client records no metadata change, and that it rejects a relative location or no location.
TestCatalogHandlersTableLocation is a new suite. It checks that the server sends table-location only for version 4 tables.
TestRESTCatalogFormatV4 is a new end-to-end suite. It loads a version 4 table without location over HTTP and appends data to it.
This test checks that the client uses the location from the catalog, and that the commit does not send the location back. It fails if the server stops sending table-location.

Coverage from the current suites
The current parser tests and REST suites use tables with format versions 1 to 3. They pass with no change, which shows that responses for these versions are the same as before.

body:
Flink INSERT OVERWRITE on a partitioned table replaces only the partitions that receive new rows. So a batch job that rebuilds a whole table cannot drop a partition that the new run no longer produces.
This PR adds an overwrite mode, static, in which the Flink sink replaces every row of the table in one snapshot. The name is the one Spark uses.
Example. A table has one file per day for 10-26, 10-27 and 10-28. The query returns rows for 10-27 and 10-28 only. Both results come from the manual test linked below.
INSERT OVERWRITE t /*+ OPTIONS('overwrite-mode'='static') */
SELECT ...;  -- rows for 10-27 and 10-28

Mode
Files deleted
Row for 10-26

dynamic (default, no hint)
2 of 3
stays

static
3 of 3
removed

Related: #9644
How the mode is set

Order
Where
How

1
Write option
SQL hint /*+ OPTIONS('overwrite-mode'='static') */, or .set("overwrite-mode", "static") on the sink builder

2
Flink config
In SQL: SET 'overwrite-mode' = 'static';

The first one that is set is used. With nothing set, the mode is dynamic, as before this PR.
What static mode does

Batch only. In SQL, INSERT OVERWRITE already fails in streaming mode. A DataStream job must set execution.runtime-mode to BATCH. AUTOMATIC is rejected, also when every source is bounded.
A query with no rows empties the table. The snapshot operation is delete. This is a choice: it matches Spark's static overwrite, and a rebuild from an empty source leaves an empty table.
A PARTITION clause is rejected. This also holds when the overwrite comes from the write option overwrite-enabled on an INSERT INTO. Spark's static overwrite replaces only that partition.

Limitations

Dynamic Iceberg sink. This sink rejects overwrite-mode=static, also when overwrite is off. So a session-level SET 'overwrite-mode' = 'static' also fails an INSERT INTO on a dynamic sink table. Support for static in this sink is follow-up work.
Other Flink versions. This PR changes flink/v2.3 only. Once it is approved, backport PRs for Flink 2.2 and 1.20 follow.

Testing
Settings. TestFlinkWriteConf checks the write option, the Flink config, and that the write option wins when both are set. It also checks that an unknown value is rejected.
Commits. TestIcebergCommitter and TestIcebergFilesCommitter check both committers. static replaces every partition, including a file written under an older partition spec, and dynamic keeps the partitions that got no new rows. An empty static overwrite removes every row in a delete snapshot, also on a table that skips other empty commits.
DataStream jobs. TestFlinkIcebergSink and TestIcebergSink run a batch job that replaces the table, and check that a streaming job is rejected. TestDynamicIcebergSink checks that the dynamic sink rejects static.
SQL. TestFlinkTableSink covers the hint, the Flink config, the older-spec table, an empty source, and the two PARTITION rejections.
Local checks. Flink 2.3, JDK 21, on this branch after the merge with main: spotlessCheck, checkstyleMain, checkstyleTest and the seven classes above. 1376 tests, 0 failures, 131 skipped. Of the new tests, only the streaming variants of the SQL tests are skipped.
Manual test. Eight cases, eleven runs, on a Flink 2.3.0 cluster with a REST catalog, through both the v1 and the v2 sink. The setup, the build that was used and the results are in this comment.

When the sink commits to a branch (iceberg.tables.default-commit-branch or a table's commit-branch) and that branch does not exist, Coordinator.lastCommittedOffsetsForTable reads the offsets from table.snapshot(branch), which is null, so it expects {}. The commit itself resolves the parent with SnapshotUtil.latestSnapshot(TableMetadata, String), which falls back to the current snapshot when the branch ref is missing, and the offset validator then finds the connector's offsets in that snapshot's ancestry. The two disagree and every commit fails with ValidationException: ... stale offsets: Expected: {} Committed: {0=n}; the coordinator stops, the task fails again after each restart, and nothing is committed until the branch is re-created by hand. This happens in the audit-branch (WAP) workflow from the branching docs when the branch is dropped after it was published to main, when a branch with max-ref-age expires, or when a connector that wrote to main is switched to a new branch. This reads the offsets from the same snapshot the commit uses, so the first commit re-creates the branch from main and continues main's offsets; the behaviour for an existing branch or for main is unchanged.

body:
Since 1.11, workers send the table uuid in DataWritten; workers on 1.10 or earlier do not. During a rolling upgrade both kinds arrive in the same commit, and CommitState.tableCommitMap groups them by the full TableReference, whose equals includes the uuid, so one table becomes two groups. The first group's commit stores the coordinator's whole control-topic position as the table's kafka.connect.offsets, and the second group's DataWritten is then below that position and filtered out as already committed ("nothing to commit"), or, with several commit threads, fails the offset validation and is filtered on replay. The workers committed their source offsets in the same transaction as their DataWritten, so those records are never redelivered and are missing from the table. Separately, when a group decoded from a 1.10 event is committed, CommitToTable re-encodes that TableReference, which still carries the 3-field 1.10 schema, and TableReference.get throws IllegalArgumentException: Invalid field position: 3 after the snapshot has landed, so the coordinator stops on every commit that contains a 1.10 event. This groups by catalog and table name and checks the uuid of each event when committing (an event whose uuid does not match the loaded table is still skipped, as before), and builds a new TableReference for CommitToTable.
Test plan: TestCoordinator#testCommitWithEventsFromWorkersBeforeAndAfterTableUuid commits one DataWritten encoded by the released iceberg-kafka-connect-events 1.10.0 (data-written-1.10.0.b64, no table uuid) and one from the current code with the uuid, for the same table. Without the change it fails either with Expected size: 2 but was: 1 (one worker's file dropped) or with IllegalArgumentException: Invalid field position: 3, depending on which group is committed first; with it, both files are committed in one snapshot. testCommitSkipsEventsForAnotherTableUuid checks that an event carrying the uuid of a dropped and re-created table is still skipped while the current table's event in the same commit is committed. End to end, a test driving the released 1.12.0 Coordinator, Worker and SinkWriter against a real table, with the second worker's answer produced by the released 1.10.0 jars in a separate JVM, lost 3 of 6 records in 18 of 18 runs; re-encoding the same answer with the table uuid lost none, and with this change applied to the released 1.12.0 classes all 6 records were committed in 3 of 3 runs with no coordinator failure. spotlessCheck, checkstyleMain, checkstyleTest and :iceberg-kafka-connect:iceberg-kafka-connect:test (168 tests) pass; the kafka-connect-runtime integration tests (Docker) were not run.
Not addressed here: a 1.10 event cannot be matched to a table instance at all, so if a table is dropped and re-created under the same name while 1.10 events for it are pending, its files are still committed into the new table. That needs a separate decision and will be raised as an issue.

An equality delete written under a partitioned spec does not apply to data files written under a different spec. So after a partition spec change, Flink upsert and CDC jobs silently leave duplicate keys and lose deletes. This documents the limitation and a workaround: stop writers with a savepoint, change the spec, rewrite all data into the new spec, then rebuild the jobs and restore them from the savepoint.
Related: #18748
Validated with Flink 2.3: an upsert job writes 1/aaa, 2/bbb and stops with a savepoint, bucket(id, 4) is added, and the rebuilt, restored job upserts 1/ccc and deletes 2. Without the rewrite the table returns 1/aaa, 1/ccc, 2/bbb; with it, 1/ccc, on main and on a non-main branch.
title: Docs: Flink upsert/CDC after a partition spec change silently leaves duplicate keys and loses deletes

Z-order and Hilbert rewrites put each column's full ordered bytes into the curve key, so one column usually ends up deciding the order. This adds an opt-in quantization-bits option (8, 16, 24 or 32) that scales each clustered column from its rewrite group's min and max, read from file bounds, onto that many bits before interleaving. Clustered columns need bounds (metrics mode truncate or full), and string columns are rejected. With the option off, keys are unchanged. Hilbert now keeps the schema's spelling of column names, as Z-order already does, so bounds can be found under case-insensitive resolution. Spark 4.2 only for now; backports will follow.

Add forChanges() to V4ManifestReader so it emits the added, modified, deleted, and replaced entries for the snapshot a manifest reference records, rather than only live files.
Expose Tracking on ManifestFile via a new tracking() accessor. This promotes Tracking and EntryStatus` to public api types.
Test plan

Test
Purpose

1. Change selection

changesEmitsWrittenStatusesAndDropsExisting
Returns ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED, and REPLACED entries for the selected snapshot; omits unmarked EXISTING entries. Uses snapshot_id for additions, deletions, and replacements, and modified_snapshot_id for modifications. Covers an input manifest without tracking metadata.

changesScopesPhysicalNonLiveEntriesToSnapshot
Returns a current physical DELETED entry and excludes physical DELETED and REPLACED entries from earlier snapshots.

changesKeepsZeroRecordFiles
Returns a current ADDED entry even when its record count is zero.

2. Deleted and replaced positions

changesOverridesPhysicalLiveStatusWithBitmaps
Converts marked ADDED and MODIFIED entries to DELETED and REPLACED at the reference's modification snapshot, preserving assigned sequence numbers, first-row IDs, and the previous modification snapshot. Omits unmarked historical additions and modifications.

3. Deleted manifest references

changesEmitsLiveEntriesOfDeletedReference
Deletes every surviving entry of a deleted manifest reference at its deletion snapshot: emits the live entries not removed by the cumulative manifest DV, excludes entries the manifest DV already removed and entries already non-live, preserves a surviving MODIFIED entry's modification snapshot and row-level deletion vector, and ignores the reference's stale deleted/replaced position bitmaps.

changesEmitsAllLiveEntriesWithoutManifestDV
Deletes every live entry of a deleted manifest reference when the reference has no cumulative manifest DV.

4. Inheritance and manifest position

changesInheritsBeforeReclassifying
Two ADDED entries inherit sequence numbers and first-row IDs before becoming DELETED. The first entry's record count advances the second entry's row-ID range.

changesPreservesManifestPositionWhenReclassifying
A reclassified entry retains physical manifest position 1 after the entry at position 0 is omitted.

5. Manifest-reference metadata

changesReadsBitmapsFromManifestReference
A serialized MODIFIED reference retains its modification snapshot and both position bitmaps through changes-mode projection.

6. Filtering

changesFiltersDataFilesByStats
Prunes a data-file entry whose column stats cannot match the row filter; keeps an entry that has no stats.

changesKeepsManifestReferencesDespiteStatsFilter
Keeps a manifest reference whose aggregate stats cannot match the row filter, because a reference's aggregates cover only its live entries and a non-live change may lie outside them.

changesFiltersDataFilesByPartition
Prunes a data-file entry in a partition the row filter excludes.

7. Negative cases

changesRejectsNonChangeManifestReference
Rejects EXISTING and REPLACED input manifest references during reader construction.

changesRejectsModifiedReferenceWithoutModificationSnapshot
Rejects a MODIFIED input manifest reference without modified_snapshot_id during reader construction.

changesRejectsModifiedEntryWithoutModificationSnapshot
Rejects an unmarked physical MODIFIED entry without modified_snapshot_id during iteration.

forChangesIsExclusiveWithScanPlanning
Rejects changes mode combined with scan planning in either call order.

forChangesIsExclusiveWithSelectAndProject
Rejects changes mode combined with select or project, testing both APIs in either call order.

forChangesRejectsUncommittedManifest
Rejects changes mode for an uncommitted manifest.

ResolvingFileIO.io() resets the credentials of an existing delegate when they differ from the credentials of the ResolvingFileIO. The ResolvingFileIO keeps the credentials from table load.
Since #15678 and #15696, S3FileIO and GCSFileIO refresh the credentials they hold before the credentials expire. After the first refresh, each io() call resets the delegate to the credentials from table load. The reset cancels the scheduled refresh and closes the storage clients. The next file operation builds new clients from credentials that are close to expiry, so the delegate fetches credentials again. This repeats on each file operation. A FileIO serialized after a reset also carries the old credentials.
This change removes the reset from io(). setCredentials now updates the existing delegates, so new credentials from the caller still reach them. A delegate that refreshes its credentials keeps them.
This affects GCSFileIO when the catalog sends gcs.oauth2.refresh-credentials-endpoint. It affects S3FileIO when its scheduled refresh succeeds, for example when credentials.uri is set. With a REST catalog, that refresh fails today (#17810). #17912 fixes it, so S3FileIO with a REST catalog is affected once #17912 merges.
Testing: ./gradlew :iceberg-core:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.io.TestResolvingIO. The new tests delegateKeepsItsRefreshedCredentials and setCredentialsUpdatesExistingDelegates fail without this change.

body:
S3FileIO and GCSFileIO schedule a refresh of the credentials they hold (#15678, #15696), so that a FileIO serialized later carries valid credentials. A deserialized copy also schedules this refresh when it builds its storage clients.
For example, Spark broadcasts the table to executors, and each executor deserializes its own copy of the FileIO. Each copy holds the same credential expiry as the original, so all open copies send a refresh request at the same time as the original. The scheduled refresh replaces only the held credentials. It does not update the storage clients that the FileIO already built, and the held credentials matter only when the FileIO is serialized again. So a copy does not use the result.
A task that runs longer than its credentials still gets new credentials. When refresh is enabled, each storage client has its own credentials provider, VendedCredentialsProvider for S3 and OAuth2CredentialsWithRefresh for GCS. The provider fetches new credentials before the old ones expire. This change does not change that path.
This change sets a transient flag in initialize(). Only an instance with the flag schedules the refresh. Java and Kryo deserialization do not call initialize(), so copies do not schedule it.
This affects GCSFileIO when the catalog sends gcs.oauth2.refresh-credentials-endpoint. It affects S3FileIO when its scheduled refresh succeeds, for example when credentials.uri is set. With a REST catalog, that refresh fails today (#17810). #17912 fixes it, so S3FileIO with a REST catalog is affected once #17912 merges.
A delegate that a deserialized ResolvingFileIO creates calls initialize(), so it still schedules a refresh.
Related: #18817 keeps refreshed delegate credentials in ResolvingFileIO.
Testing: added deserializedCopyDoesNotScheduleRefresh to TestS3FileIOCredentialRefresh and TestGCSFileIOCredentialRefresh. It checks Java and Kryo copies.

body:
Every task's control consumer reads every event on the control topic, including the other tasks' DATA_WRITTEN replies. Those carry the full data file metadata for a commit and are by far the largest events, yet Worker decodes each one only to drop it in receive. With many tasks this decode work grows with the square of the task count and runs on the task thread. Eon's ingest-bench write-up of a 192-task run traces commit requests arriving after the commit timeout partly to this (attempted-engines.md).
This change:

adds two record headers to every control event, iceberg.connect.group-id and iceberg.connect.payload-type
adds Channel.handles(PayloadType), overridden by Worker (START_COMMIT) and Coordinator (DATA_WRITTEN, DATA_COMPLETE) to match what their receive acts on
skips a record before decoding when its group header names another connector or its type header names a type the channel does not handle. The control-topic offset still advances as before.

Records without the headers, or with a type name this version does not know, are decoded exactly as today, so a rolling upgrade with mixed versions keeps working. Older readers ignore the headers. Fetch volume is unchanged; this only removes the decode.
Test plan

headers are written on sent events (TestChannel)
events for another connector, and event types a channel does not handle, are skipped without decoding: their values are deliberately not valid Avro, so the tests fail if they are decoded, and offsets still advance (TestChannel, TestWorker)
events without headers and events with an unknown type name are still decoded (TestChannel)
a record produced by send round-trips through a reader that skips its type (TestChannel)

The new skip tests fail with the skip disabled. ./gradlew :iceberg-kafka-connect:iceberg-kafka-connect:check passes (173 tests).
Benchmark (JDK 17, Apple Silicon arm64; code: https://gist.github.com/Mohith26/c7ec146b57f6b0f5a58729a51b55975a). A DATA_WRITTEN reply with 512 data files and metrics for 100 columns (the default inferred-metrics limit) encodes to 2.0 MB, close to the ~1.5 MB replies in the run above.

median

decode one reply
46.9 ms

worker consumes 48 replies + 1 START_COMMIT, no headers (decode all)
2078.6 ms

same, with headers (skip)
0.4 ms

7 runs after 2 warm-ups, in-process MockConsumer, so this measures decode cost only, not fetch.
This change was written with AI assistance; the tests and benchmark above were run locally before opening. The part worth a closer look is keeping handles in sync with receive in the two subclasses.
title: Kafka Connect: Skip control events a channel ignores without decoding them

body:
When OverwriteFiles (Spark copy-on-write) or RowDelta replaces data files under a conflict detection filter, concurrent deletes are pruned by that filter. An equality delete outside the filter is missed when it applies to a replaced file, so deleted rows reappear. This affects Spark copy-on-write DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE, which set the conflict detection filter from their scan filter, when they race an equality delete writer such as a Flink upsert job. Replaced files are now checked without the filter, so such commits fail with a conflict. These commits may now read delete manifests outside the filter's partitions, as unfiltered overwrites already do. The FILE_DAY_2_ANOTHER_RANGE_EQ_DELETES fixture now declares its equality field ID, because the non-conflicting case is now decided by the delete's id range instead of the filter.
Repro: file with id 5..9, conflictDetectionFilter(id = 5), concurrent equality delete for id = 7. Before: commits, and the delete stops applying to rewritten id 7. After: found new delete for replaced data file.
Test plan: new TestOverwriteWithValidation and TestRowDelta cases (v2, v3) fail on main and pass here.
title: Core: Fix deleted rows reappearing when copy-on-write races an equality delete

Spark decides at planning time whether a scan is vectorized, using the shred table property, metrics mode and variant lower bounds. When a file is shredded but none of those say so (for example, shredded arrays, which write no variant bounds, with shredding enabled through the session conf), the vectorized reader fails with Unsupported variant: shredded typed_value .... This follows #18434: VectorizedReaderBuilder now checks each file's variant group, and a shredded group is read by the existing row-based VariantReaderBuilder into the same metadata/value vectors the unshredded path produces. Nested shredded variants without field ids are skipped, as before. planningOpensOnlyRoot
Planning opens and closes the root while leaving leaf readers unopened until a result accessor is called.

The first accessor loads the changes and closes every opened reader before returning. Repeated access opens no additional readers.

Groups four distinct ADDED, DELETED, MODIFIED, and REPLACED files into their corresponding change collections.

removedVersionsRetainStats
Preserves projected stats on removed and replaced data-file versions for later validation.

colocatedDVsAreNotStandaloneDeleteFiles
Retains a data file's deletion-vector descriptor without reporting standalone delete-file additions or removals.

Any of the six accessors can trigger loading. The input is traversed and closed once; subsequent accesses reuse the results.

An iteration failure closes the input and is rethrown by subsequent accessors without another read or close.

body:
Adds reusable wrappers that write a TrackedFile, with the tracking supplied by the writer, using the v4 tracked file schema.
The leaf wrapper accepts only data files and writes tracking as given so unassigned sequence numbers and first row IDs are inherited on read, rejecting null sequence numbers that cannot be inherited.
The root wrapper requires the tracking to carry a snapshot ID and writes the sequence numbers, manifest min sequence number, and first row ID that the spec requires in the root manifest, assigning the commit's values to files added by the commit. Both project spec partitions to the union partition type when writing, and write a null spec ID and partition for files whose spec has no partition fields, as the v4 spec requires for unpartitioned files.
Content stats are written through a view laid out by the manifest's content stats type, so stats from any ContentStats implementation, including MapBackedContentStats adapted from DataFile metrics, are written at the correct positions.
Test plan:
These tests call get on the wrappers directly, using mocked TrackedFile and Tracking, and cover only the values the wrappers substitute and the checks in wrap. They don't test get-by-position for every field: the wrappers will be embedded in the v4 leaf and root manifest writers, whose round-trip tests will write and read back every field and catch any position mismatch with the schema.
Partition projection, content stats, and sequence number validation are implemented once in code shared by both wrappers, so they are tested through the leaf wrapper only. The root wrapper is tested for the behavior only it has: the commit values it assigns, the snapshot ID it requires, first-row-id assignment, and manifest entries.

Substitutions

Null spec ID and partition for unpartitioned files and for specs with only void transforms
Partitions are projected to the union partition type
Missing field stats and missing stats counts are written as null
Root writes the commit sequence number as the min sequence number of a new manifest
Leaf writes null sequence numbers and first-row-id for an added file
Root writes the commit sequence numbers and the assigned first-row-id for an added data file or data manifest
Leaf keeps a null data sequence number for a file modified in the commit, so it is inherited on read
Root writes the commit data sequence number for a file modified in the commit, keeping its file sequence number

Validations

Construction rejects a union partition type missing a spec's partition field
Leaf accepts only data files; both wrappers reject delete files
Data files must not have manifest info; manifests require manifest info and must not have a deletion vector
Unknown spec IDs are rejected
Root requires a snapshot ID
Tracking first-row-id must be null for added files and present otherwise
Root first-row-id is assigned only to added data files and data manifests, never to existing files or delete manifests
A null data sequence number is only allowed for added or modified files from the committing snapshot, including a leaf written with no commit snapshot ID
A null file sequence number is only allowed for files added in the committing snapshot

body:
After a partition field is added and then dropped (e.g., when a partition change gets rolled back), the table goes back to its old spec ID. Streaming reads can then silently skip the first append after the revert. With async planning enabled, the stream can instead hang permanently, even across restarts.
The cause: Manifest merging writes the commit's manifest for the dropped spec first, and it only holds existing files. Micro-batch positions count those files, but the planners end the snapshot at its added-file count. This change fixes the end position in each planner while keeping their numbering, so existing checkpoints still resume correctly.
Repro: add a partition field, append 1 and 2, drop the field, append 3 and then 4, then stream from the beginning. Before: 1, 2, 4. After: 1, 2, 3, 4.

body:
Problem
A spherical geography edge follows a minor great-circle arc. Its latitude can reach a maximum or minimum between the endpoints, so a box built from endpoint coordinates can exclude part of the edge.
For example, the arc from A = (0°, 60°) to B = (90°, 60°), in (longitude, latitude) order, reaches about 67.7923°N at 45°E. Both endpoints are at 60°N. Geography file statistics need to cover the full arc before they can support safe pruning.

The purple box includes outward numerical padding. Its north bound is approximately 67.7923525°N; the padding is too small to see at this scale.
Algorithm
The package-private builder accumulates points and minor great-circle edges into a BoundingBox.

Longitude: Merge the longitude intervals covered by the edges. Longitude is circular, so a box that crosses the antimeridian stores west > east.
Latitude: Convert the endpoints to 3D unit vectors. Their cross product defines the great-circle plane. For a non-equatorial great circle, project the north pole onto that plane and normalize to find the northern latitude extremum; the opposite point gives the southern candidate. Include only candidates on the edge's minor arc, together with the endpoint latitudes.
Numerical handling: Pad accepted extrema outward to guard against rounding. When the cross product is very small, the endpoint dot product distinguishes short arcs from nearly antipodal edges. Short arcs receive conservative latitude padding; unresolved nearly antipodal edges use world bounds.

Coincident endpoints are treated as a point. Pole vertices retain their stored longitude. NaN ordinates do not contribute to their dimension. Empty input or a missing dimension produces no bounds. Out-of-range or infinite coordinates permanently suppress bounds, including after a world-bounds fallback.
Scope
This PR provides the bounds calculation for spherical points and edges. WKB traversal, polygon interior bounds, writer integration, and scan planning are separate work.
Part of #18705. Related spherical bounds implementation: #17788.
Test plan

Check analytical northern and southern extrema, reversed edges, antimeridian crossings, poles, and degenerate inputs.
Reproduce rounding undercoverage for short arcs and extrema near the equator. Check the near-antipodal fallback boundary.
Check NaN handling, invalid coordinates, empty input, and suppression after invalid input.
Check that sampled points along seeded random minor arcs lie within the returned bounds.

All 89 spherical tests and 16 longitude tests pass on Java 17. Core Spotless and Checkstyle main/test pass.

body:
Iceberg's Spark integration has no way for an accelerated reader or compaction runner to take over the per-file work while Iceberg keeps planning, delete resolution and commits. This adds two extension points to Spark 4.2, both inactive unless a provider is named: PartitionReaderFactoryProvider (session conf spark.sql.iceberg.partition-reader-factory-provider, read option partition-reader-factory-provider), which wraps the batch scan's reader factory and delegates task groups it cannot serve, with a public HasScanTaskGroup, a capability interface on InputPartition in the style of Spark's HasPartitionKey, exposing the task group, table, IO, projection and case sensitivity; and FileRewriteRunnerProvider (spark.sql.iceberg.rewrite-runner-provider, action option rewrite-runner-provider), which supplies the bin-pack rewrite_data_files runner. Summary
Fixes #18758 by preventing a transaction with directly staged metadata from reporting success after a concurrent commit silently discards its changes.
RESTCatalogAdapter.commitTransaction stages changes through CatalogHandlers.commit on transaction TableOperations, without registering a PendingUpdate. After a conflicting commit, BaseTransaction.applyUpdates refreshes the table and replays an empty pending-update list, discarding the intended write and potentially returning success.

body:
Description
Fixes #18902.
When a REST commit request fails after it has been sent (no response, a connection reset, a read
timeout), HTTPClient wraps the IOException in a plain RESTException. The server may have
applied the commit, but the client reports an ordinary failure: it never raises
CommitStateUnknownException, and RESTTableOperations never tries the reconciliation it already
does for 5xx responses. A caller that retries the failed operation then commits it twice.
This change reports a transport failure on a commit request as CommitStateUnknownException, so it
is handled like a 5xx. Snapshot-add-only commits are reconciled, and other commits are reported as
unknown rather than failed. Failures that happen before anything is sent (refused connection,
connect or connection-pool timeout, unknown host, no route to host, TLS handshake failure) stay a
RESTException. The conversion applies only to commit requests, not to HTTPClient as a whole,
which was the concern raised in #6778.
One visible change in behaviour: create and replace transactions (for example CTAS and RTAS) are not
reconciled, so a lost response to their commit now raises CommitStateUnknownException instead of
RESTException. Callers that retried on RESTException will stop retrying it, which is the intent:
the table may already have been created or replaced.
Changes

Add RESTTableOperations.commitRequest, which converts a RESTException caused by an
IOException into a CommitStateUnknownException, unless the failure happened before the request
was sent. The default is unknown: reporting a commit that was applied as failed invites a retry
that applies it twice, while reporting one that wasn't as unknown at worst leaves orphan files.
Use it for table commits in RESTTableOperations.commit, so the existing reconciliation also
covers lost responses.
Use it for multi-table commits in RESTSessionCatalog.commitTransaction.
Add regression tests in TestRESTCatalog:

testReconcileOnLostCommitResponse: the server applies an append but the response is lost; the
commit is reconciled and succeeds.
testLostCommitResponseIsCommitStateUnknown: a read timeout, no response, or a connection
reset on a commit that can't be reconciled raises CommitStateUnknownException.
testCommitThatWasNeverSentIsNotCommitStateUnknown: each failure that happens before sending
stays a RESTException.
testLostTransactionResponseIsCommitStateUnknown: the same for a multi-table transaction.

Validation

Core tests (:iceberg-core:test): passed.
:iceberg-core:build -x test (Checkstyle, Error Prone, Spotless), revapi and javadoc: passed.
git diff --check: passed.
End to end, with Spark 3.5 against apache/iceberg-rest-fixture and a proxy that forwards one
commit and then drops the connection (the reproduction in #18902): with this change applied to
1.12.0, the INSERT reports success and the row is committed once; without it, the INSERT
fails with RESTException although the row was committed.

Notes for reviewers

The before-sending list is explicit; any other IOException is treated as possibly sent. A
pre-send failure missing from the list would be reported as unknown, which is safe (orphan files
at worst), whereas the opposite mistake would bring back this bug.
Unrelated to this change, but noticed while testing: Tasks treats any InterruptedIOException
other than SocketTimeoutException as a thread interruption, so a connection-pool timeout
(ConnectionRequestTimeoutException) during a commit sets the caller's interrupt flag. The
before-sending test therefore calls commitRequest directly.
I haven't checked how this interacts with the HTTP client's own retry strategy. In the end-to-end
run, the commit request reached the catalog only once.
The end-to-end check used a Spark runtime built from 1.12.0 with this change, not one built from
main.

body:
Closes #18901
SparkBatch.planInputPartitions() broadcasts the table and the FileIO on every call, and SparkScan.toBatch() returns a new SparkBatch each time. Spark plans input partitions for every copy of a scan node, during planning. When dynamic partition pruning filters nest over a chain of joins on a partition column, the number of copies is exponential and each leaves two broadcasts in the driver until the plan is released. A production query with 10 such joins created 264,382 broadcasts and exhausted driver memory before starting a stage. This PR creates the broadcasts once per scan and shares them between its batches. It does not change how many subqueries Spark plans.
Backports to Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 will follow once this change is merged.
Test plan (TestScanBroadcastReuse):

Planning input partitions again for the same scan creates no new broadcasts. This is the behavior the change adds.
A six-way left join on the partition column with DPP enabled stays below the number of nested filters (2^6). This checks that Spark shares one scan between the plan copies, which the fix depends on. Without the change the query creates more than 400 broadcasts.

body: AuthSession.fromTokenResponse() and refresh() set the session's expiresAtMillis only from the exp claim of a JWT access token; expires_in from the token response was used to schedule the background refresh but never stored on the session. This falls back to startTime + expires_in when the token is not a JWT (RFC 6749 §5.1), in both places. testCatalogTokenRefreshFailsAndUsesCredentialForRefresh drops from two token-exchange attempts to one: with the expiry known, the retry sees the 1 s token as expired and goes straight to the credential flow, as that branch intends.

body:
This PR supersedes #17901 by @fmorillo7694. It keeps their original commit, rebases it onto main, and addresses the open review comment. All credit for the fix and the regression test goes to them. If they'd rather continue in #17901, I'm happy to close this PR.
Problem
IcebergCommitter reads getMaxCommittedCheckpointId() once, before the commit. Another commit for the same checkpoint can land after that read, and the second commit then applies cleanly on top of the first. The checkpoint's files are committed twice. See #17901 and #14425 for the original analysis and the deterministic reproduction.
We also hit this in production with blue/green deployments, where the old job keeps running for a short time after the savepoint is taken. The old job commits checkpoint N. Seconds later, the new job commits the same committable, which it restored from the savepoint, under the same job ID. In one table, we found 10 data files that were each added twice, in consecutive snapshots.
Changes
The first commit is the original change from #17901, rebased onto main. The second commit makes these changes:

Moves MaxCommittedCheckpointIdValidator into SinkUtil, as @mxm asked in #17901 (comment). Its mismatch exception moves with it.
Adapts the validator to #18303. DynamicCommitter now identifies its own snapshots by sink ID, and IcebergCommitter still uses the job ID and operator ID. So each caller now passes a predicate that matches its own snapshot summaries.
In IcebergCommitter, validates only after a restore. This matches the up-front check since #18123. After a stateless start, a job can reuse its job ID while its checkpoint IDs start from 1 again. Without this condition, the validator would skip those commits and silently drop data. testCommitTxnAfterStatelessRestart caught this. Duplicate commits come from restored committables, so restored jobs, including blue/green deployments, are still protected.
Updates the regression test for the new IcebergCommitter constructor.

Like #17901, this targets Flink 2.3 only. Backports can follow once the approach is approved.
Testing

TestIcebergCommitterDuplicateCommit passes. It fails when the validator is disabled, with 2 snapshots instead of 1.
TestIcebergCommitter (336), TestIcebergFilesCommitter (96), TestIcebergSink (312), TestDynamicCommitter (14) and TestDynamicIcebergSink (50) all pass.
spotlessCheck, checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest pass.
title: Flink: Validate concurrent commits in IcebergSink to prevent commit duplication

body:
SortOrder#satisfies compares the two orders field by field with SortField#satisfies. That allows a finer transform to stand in for a coarser one, such as ts for day(ts). This is only valid for the last field of the order being satisfied.
When another field follows, rows that tie on the coarse value must still be ordered by the next field. Sorting by [ts, symbol] orders the rows within a day by ts first. symbol is not ordered within the day, so the data is not sorted by [day(ts), symbol]. Before this change, [ts, symbol].satisfies([day(ts), symbol]) returned true.
This change requires every field of the other order except the last to match exactly (equals). Only the last field may be satisfied by a finer transform:

this
other
before
after

[ts]
[day(ts)]
true
true

[symbol, ts]
[symbol, day(ts)]
true
true

[ts, symbol]
[day(ts), symbol]
true
false

Impact: SortOrder#satisfies is public API and nothing in this repo calls it from main code. An engine that uses it to decide whether existing data is already sorted could skip a needed sort and write wrongly ordered output. Callers affected by this change will now do the sort they previously skipped. SortOrderUtil calls Transform#satisfiesOrderOf directly, stops after the first non-matching field, and is unaffected.
Tests: added TestSortOrder#testSatisfiesTransformFollowedByAnotherField.
AI disclosure: AI assistance was used in this PR. I reviewed the logic and ran TestSortOrder.
title: API: Fix SortOrder#satisfies for transforms followed by other fields

body:
Closes #19002
This PR improves file pruning for IN predicates on columns that use non-order-preserving partition transforms such as bucket.
Partition projection already limits a manifest scan to matching bucket values. File metrics evaluation, however, still evaluates every literal in the original IN predicate against every selected file. A literal assigned to another bucket can therefore retain a file that cannot contain that literal. Lists above the metrics evaluator's 200-value limit also skip bounds evaluation before literals are narrowed to the file's partition.
Change

InclusiveMetricsEvaluator.forRowFilter(Expression, PartitionSpec, boolean) binds the row filter once and indexes each IN predicate's literals by transformed partition value. The name and argument order follow ManifestEvaluator.forRowFilter. The existing schema-only constructors are unchanged and behave as an unpartitioned spec.
The index lives in a new package-private class, PartitionedInLiterals, with two operations: build(boundExpr, spec) once per evaluator and literalsFor(literalSet, partition) once per file. It knows nothing about files or stats, so other evaluators can reuse it.
For each file, metrics evaluation compares only the literals that map to the file's partition value. A file with a null partition value for that field is skipped, because IN never matches null.
Only partition fields whose transform does not preserve order (in practice bucket) narrow literals. identity and truncate fields are ignored, and all other predicates are evaluated as before. When a column has several such fields, the first one is used.
InclusiveEvalVisitor gets a protected literals(Set<T>) hook that in() calls before the 200-value limit and the bounds loop. The default returns the full set, so the base class still owns IN evaluation and each evaluator only decides which literals apply to its current input.
ManifestReader opts into the partition-aware path, so data and delete manifests (via DeleteFileIndex) both benefit.

Only planning-time file selection changes. Files that can contain a match are never removed. The 200-value limit now applies after narrowing; a general fix for the limit on unpartitioned columns is out of scope and could follow as a separate PR.
v4 planning
InclusiveStatsEvaluator (used by V4ManifestReader, which is not yet reachable from a table scan) extends the same base visitor, so it inherits the hook with the all-literals default and is unchanged by this PR. Once v4 planning is wired up, the same narrowing can be added without copying code:

V4ManifestReader already has specsById, and every TrackedFile carries specId() and partition(). Build one PartitionedInLiterals per spec in the evaluator's constructor, and pass the file's spec ID and partition into eval alongside its ContentStats.
StatsEvalVisitor then overrides the hook as literals(set) = indexesBySpec.get(specId).literalsFor(set, partition).

I left that for a follow-up because the v4 reader is still in progress (#17159, #17201) and the eval signature there is still settling.
Validation

./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-core:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.TestManifestReader
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-api:revapi :iceberg-api:javadoc :iceberg-api:checkstyleMain :iceberg-api:checkstyleTest :iceberg-core:checkstyleMain :iceberg-core:checkstyleTest :iceberg-api:spotlessCheck :iceberg-core:spotlessCheck

TestManifestReader covers format versions 1 through 4: ordinary and 250-value IN predicates on data manifests, equality-delete mani […]

body:
Part 2 of #17919, following #18252.
A file column's six nested fields take the IDs immediately after its own, so the type must stay in step with the field that holds it and those IDs must never go to another column. This PR enforces that in schema construction and evolution. UpdateSchema.addColumn now gives a file column, at any depth, a base ID that matches its field and reserves the derived block so later columns cannot collide. Replacing a table reserves the block when a column becomes a file. Committing file columns still needs schema JSON serialization, which comes in Part 3, and unionByNameWith support for file columns comes in Part 4.
API changes (no new public methods)

Schema rejects a file column whose type's base ID differs from its field ID. A column that takes a reserved ID is rejected by the existing duplicate-ID check.
CheckCompatibility accepts reading a file as a file and reports any other type as incompatible.
A TypeUtil.GetID that implements only get(int) works with file columns as long as it keeps each file field's ID, and throws if it would reassign one.

Core changes

UpdateSchema rejects renaming, deleting, promoting, or changing the requirement, doc, or default of a file's nested fields.
MetricsConfig treats a file's uri, size, and content_type like any other column: they get the inferred or configured default mode and count toward the inferred column limit. Its offset, checksum, and inline default to counts, or none when the default mode is none. SchemaOrder visits a file like a struct. Table metadata creation reaches both after #18269 and #18331.

Series

Part 1 (merged): #18252
Part 2: this PR
The following parts are draft branches in my fork. They are not open PRs and will change as this one is reviewed. Each link shows only that part's diff against the previous part.
Part 3: Core: Serialize the file type in schema JSON
Part 4: API, Core, Data: Handle the file type in type switches and struct views
Part 5: Core: Read and write file columns in Avro
Part 6: Parquet: Map the file type to a group
Part 7: ORC: Support the file type in schema conversion and visitors
Part 8: Hive, Kafka Connect, AWS, Arrow: Render a file column as a struct
