body:
Bumps datamodel-code-generator from 0.87.0 to 0.91.0.

Release notes
Sourced from datamodel-code-generator's releases.

0.91.0
Breaking Changes
Code Generation Changes

Empty unused classes for x-python-import schemas referenced outside $defs are no longer generated - Some schemas carry x-python-import, are reached through a JSON pointer outside $defs or definitions (for example /components/Options in the same file or other.json plus /components/Options), and are named only by fields. Previously such a schema was also written as an empty class that nothing used, such as class Options(BaseModel): pass, next to the import that types those fields. That class is now left out, which matches how these schemas are already handled in $defs. Fields that reference the schema still use the imported class, such as OrderedDict. A schema that another model uses as a base, including the subclasses made by --reuse-model, keeps its model. Code that imported or referenced the removed empty class from the generated module must be updated. (#6415)
Nested model names under --naming-strategy enclosing-model now follow the restored owner name in modular output - When several input files each define a model with the same name (for example Parent), the naming plan numbers the later one across the input and its own module then gives it back its base name. Models whose names were composed from that numbered owner (inline children, grandchildren, ordinal, tagged or composed models) now also take the name composed from the restored name, e.g. ParentChild and ParentChildGrand instead of names built from the numbered owner such as Parent1Child, wherever the module leaves those names free. Code that imports or references the previously generated nested class names must be updated. Default naming is unaffected (#6417)
Schemas with items or prefixItems but no array type are no longer typed as lists - JsonSchemaObject.is_array now treats a schema as an array only when its type is array, when array is in its type list and items are given, or when it has items but no declared type. Before, any items or prefixItems made the schema an array. A schema like {"type": ["string", "null"], "items": {...}} used to produce list[int] | None and now produces str | None. {"type": "string", "items": ...} now produces str. {"type": ["object", "null"], "items": ..., "properties": ...} now produces Object | None instead of a union that also included list[int]. {"type": ["integer", "boolean"], "prefixItems": ...} now produces int | bool instead of list[Any]. The old output rejected every valid value, but the field types in generated models, root models and type aliases change, so code that relied on the old list types may need updating (#6419)
Constraints on patternProperties values are now kept on a generated type alias - For Pydantic v2 output (BaseModel and dataclass), a patternProperties value schema used to be parsed without a field, so its constraints were dropped. Now, when the dict key type rejects every key that matches none of the patterns and no value is Any, those constraints go on a new type alias named after the parent model with a PatternProperty suffix, for example PArrPatternProperty = TypeAliasType("PArrPatternProperty", Annotated[list[str], Field(min_length=2)]). In every mode, including the default options, this applies to the minItems/maxItems of an array value. Under --field-constraints and --use-annotated (as in the presets), it also applies to bounds, lengths and pattern. As a result, dict value hints change from dict[constr(pattern=r'^a'), list[str]] to dict[constr(pattern=r'^a'), PArrPatternProperty], modules gain the new alias names plus TypeAliasType/Annotated imports, a Pydantic dataclass can switch to @dataclass(config=ConfigDict(regex_engine="python-re")) when the alias holds a lookahead pattern, and data that breaks the value's schema constraints but validated before is now rejected (#6424)

Release notes
Sourced from mkdocs-material's releases.

mkdocs-material-9.8.1

[!WARNING]
Material for MkDocs reaches end of life on May 5, 2027. Critical fixes and security updates continue until that date.
We're continuing our work with Zensical, a maintained successor built by the team behind Material for MkDocs. It carries forward what we've learned from building documentation tools with this community, with Markdown authoring, a familiar design, and full control over your content. Zensical is Open Source and MIT-licensed.
You can evaluate Zensical alongside MkDocs using your existing mkdocs.yml. Check plugin compatibility and compare your pages, navigation, search, and customizations before switching. The classic theme variant preserves the appearance of Material for MkDocs. See the migration guide for the steps and current compatibility details.
Upcoming changes on November 5

Updated Docker base image to Alpine 3.24
Updated Docker image dependencies to fix vulnerabilities
Updated Node build-time dependencies to fix vulnerabilities

Changelog
Sourced from mkdocs-material's changelog.

mkdocs-material-9.8.1 (2026-11-07)

Updated Docker base image to Alpine 3.24
Updated Docker image dependencies to fix vulnerabilities
Updated Node build-time dependencies to fix vulnerabilities

mkdocs-material-9.8.0 (2026-10-24)
This is primarily a security release. It raises dependency minimums to
address known vulnerabilities. We recommend upgrading to this release and
updating your dependency lockfiles.
Python 3.11 or newer is now required. Python 3.8–3.10 are no longer supported.

Updated Node build-time dependencies to fix vulnerabilities
Updated Python dependency minimums and required Python 3.11
Removed RSS from recommended dependencies
Updated project status and maintenance links
Updated CLI notice with end-of-life and migration guidance
Removed redirects from recommended dependencies

Previous dependency ranges allowed versions with known vulnerabilities. The new
minimums cover core Python dependencies and the optional git and imaging
extras, including GitPython 3.2.1 or newer for the git extra.
Recent releases of mkdocs-rss-plugin and mkdocs-redirects depend on ProperDocs,
a separate static site generator that Material for MkDocs does not require.
Removing these plugins from the recommended extra keeps its dependency
footprint smaller and leaves the choice of additional tools to each project.
If your project uses RSS feeds or redirects, declare the relevant plugin
explicitly in your own dependencies.
The CLI notice now gives the May 5, 2027 end-of-life date and links to the
Zensical migration guide:
https://zensical.org/docs/compatibility/mkdocs/migration/
It also clarifies that third-party ProperDocs migration notices do not represent
a recommendation from the Material for MkDocs team. Package metadata now marks
the project as inactive and includes maintenance and migration links.

body:
FLOAT binding folds comparisons against finite out-of-range DOUBLE literals to constants and treats double infinities as out of range. This can misclassify NaN, infinite, and null values. Keep ordering comparisons against the appropriate finite float endpoint, and preserve infinities when converting double literals to float.
Fixes #18700.
Test plan: compare FLOAT evaluation with equivalent DOUBLE evaluation for ordering, equality, and IN/NOT IN predicates, including finite limits, infinities, NaN, and null; verify literal conversion and binding shapes. All 9 new regression cases fail before the fix. The API module check reports 1351 tests, 1 skipped, and no failures/errors. Formatting, production/test Checkstyle, and module assembly pass.

AI Disclosure

Model: GPT-6.
Platform/Tool: OpenAI Codex generated the implementation, regression tests, and this description.
Human Oversight: unreviewed.
Prompt Summary: fix the float literal and predicate binding problem reported in #18700 and validate the API module.
title: API: Preserve float comparisons with wide literals

body:
This adds V4ManifestWriter to produce v4 manifests. There are two inner classes to produce leaf and root manifests (created using createRoot and createLeaf). The root writer is similar to ManifestListWriter.
Like ManifestWriter, this class assumes that incoming entry/tracking metadata is unchanged and replaces it with updated metadata produced by TrackingBuilder. This API accepts TrackedFile because the writer is not responsible for wrapping and is will be used directly by writers that handle TrackedFile. For instance, copying or filtering manifests will work with TrackedFile directly.
The API for adding files is:

append(TrackedFile) adds a new file to the manifest
appendAtSeq(TrackedFile, long) adds a new file with a given data sequence number; equivalent to ManifestWriter.add(file, seq)
modify(TrackedFile, DeletionVector) adds a deletion vector to an existing data file
existing(TrackedFile) adds an existing file to the manifest
delete(TrackedFile) adds a file as deleted
replace(TrackedFile) adds a file as replaced

These methods work with manifest files, but this PR is focused on data files and tests only that surface area. This also does not include support for updating column files, but writes with column files are validated.
Test plan:

Test data file cases only

With and without DV
Unpartitioned and partitioned in the same file

Test all statuses (added, modified, existing, deleted, replaced)

Test append at sequence number
Test append with DV
Test modify with new DV

Test root and leaf files

Root metadata is written into the file and read unchanged
Leaf metadata is written as null and inherited in the manifest reader
Leaf files may be written with a null snapshot ID for manifest append cases

Validate

All tracking fields
All data file fields except key metadata
First row ID assignment (data files) in the root increments by file.recordCount()
Leaf manifest info produced by the writer: counts using all of the API methods, min sequence number
title: Core: Add V4ManifestWriter

Adds a JMH benchmark that reads single leaves at depth 1-3 of a wide nested struct, plus struct+child and whole-struct selections, and reports bytes read per op as a JMH counter. Before #18336 a deep leaf read its whole intermediate struct; this makes that visible, and it matters because local timing barely moves when the extra columns are fetched but not decoded. The #18336 results are in that PR.
Results (Spark 4.1, JDK 17, local FS, 10 files x 100k rows, 690 MB, SingleShotTime, 5 measured invocations; cd3ae3c80 before #18336 vs 843d36de after):

Timing is only comparable within a run pair: the same commit drifted 24% on the slowest arm (2.48 to 3.08 s/op) between two runs, while its bytes moved 0.3%. Anything smaller than that drift has to be argued in bytes, not seconds.
Reading it: pruned arms are compared against same-type baselines, so readDepth3Leaf (a long at depth 3) is expected to cost about what readId (a long at the top level) costs, and readDepth1Leaf about what readDepth2Leaf does; every leaf is orders of magnitude below readWholeStruct. Before the fix, the depth-3 leaf read exactly what person.l2, person.l2.x reads, which is the whole l2 subtree.
bytes is a @AuxCounters(AuxCounters.Type.EVENTS) column, so it appears next to the timing in the JMH results file and excludes warmup. Each measured invocation resets it and reads one op, so the score is the sum over the five measured invocations and scorePercentiles carries the per-op bytes. Type.OPERATIONS is not usable here: in SingleShotTime mode it drops the column entirely. The value is read from /proc/self/io rchar, which counts read syscalls rather than Hadoop FS statistics (those miss Parquet reads entirely); it is Linux-only, and elsewhere the counter logs once and reports nothing. A per-op floor fails the run when the counter sees an implausibly small read, so a blind counter cannot be mistaken for a pruned read.
Test plan: ran the benchmark on main and on the parent of 843d36de, and re-ran it on this branch.

body:
This PR introduces CanonicalUriFileIO, a wrapper around Iceberg's FileIO abstraction that decouples the URI stored in Iceberg table metadata from the physical URI used to access files.
It allows different compute engines to access the same Iceberg table using different storage protocols while retaining a consistent canonical URI representation in table metadata.
What does this change?

Canonical URI resolution: Resolves canonical URIs stored in Iceberg metadata into protocol-specific physical URIs at runtime using configurable URI mappings.
FileIO delegation: Delegates actual filesystem operations to a configured underlying FileIO implementation.
Consistent URI handling: Applies URI resolution across metadata files, manifest lists, manifests, data files, and delete files.
Relative path support: Handles relative and absolute file paths while preserving Iceberg's path representation semantics across table format versions.
Configurable mappings: Allows storage-specific URI mappings to be configured without introducing dependencies on any particular storage system or filesystem implementation.

Compatibility

Existing Iceberg tables can be accessed without rewriting their metadata.
Existing fully-qualified file locations continue to work.
When canonical URI resolution is not configured, existing FileIO behavior remains unchanged.
No changes to the Iceberg table format specification or catalog interfaces are required.

Reference : #18921
title: Core: Add CanonicalUriFileIO for canonical-to-physical URI mapping

body:
Closes #17288
Problem
With spark_catalog set to SparkSessionCatalog over a Hive catalog, reading an Iceberg view that has column aliases fails:
CREATE VIEW v (c1, c2) AS VALUES (1, 2);
SELECT * FROM v;
-- [INCOMPATIBLE_VIEW_SCHEMA_CHANGE] The SQL query of view `spark_catalog`.`default`.`v` has an incompatible
-- schema change and column c1 cannot be resolved. Expected 1 columns named c1 but got [].
WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION from the issue isn't required. The column aliases are what trigger it.
The Hive catalog stores Iceberg views in the Hive Metastore as VIRTUAL_VIEWs.

SparkSessionCatalog.loadTable fails to load the view as an Iceberg table and falls back to the session catalog.
The session catalog returns the metastore entry as a Hive view (V1Table).
Spark's ResolveRelations then resolves it as a v1 view before the ResolveViews rule of the Iceberg extensions gets to it.
SessionCatalog.fromCatalogTable looks up each view column by name in the output of the view's query. Without the view.query.out.col.* properties that Spark writes for its own views, it looks for the view's column names (c1). The query only outputs col1 and col2, so the lookup fails.

Iceberg views are also missed by the rest of the Iceberg view handling in this setup: DESCRIBE, SHOW CREATE TABLE, the schema binding mode, temp object checks, and others.
Fix
In SparkSessionCatalog.loadTable, the session catalog's result is not returned when it is a view that the Iceberg view catalog knows (viewExists). The original NoSuchTableException is rethrown instead, so ResolveViews resolves the view as an Iceberg view, the same as for the other catalogs. The extra viewExists call is only made when the session catalog returns a view. Hive views that aren't Iceberg views are still resolved by Spark, because HiveCatalog.viewExists is false for them.
Testing

New TestSessionCatalogHiveViews covers SparkSessionCatalog with type=hive, which TestViews doesn't cover. It has three tests:

column aliases over VALUES
the exact SQL from the issue, with WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION
aliases with a column comment over a table

All three fail without the fix with the error above.

Locally, I also ran TestViews with only the SparkSessionCatalog + Hive configuration as its parameter. That run isn't part of this PR.

Without the fix, 26 of its 86 tests fail.
With the fix, 25 of those pass and no new failures appear.
The remaining one, renameViewToDifferentTargetCatalog, fails with or without the fix. HiveCatalog.renameView rejects the three-part target identifier, which is a separate issue.

On Spark 4.2, TestSparkSessionCatalog, TestViews, TestViewCatalogCache, TestReferencedByViewChain, TestTempViewRefresh and TestSessionCatalogHiveViews pass.

Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 have the same code. I'll backport in a follow-up once this is reviewed.
title: Spark 4.2: Resolve Iceberg views in SparkSessionCatalog backed by Hive as Iceberg views

Closes #18952.
SPARK-60044 freezes the ordering of a planned GroupPartitionsExec k-way merge. Before it, turning spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.partitionKeyOrdering.enabled off after planning emptied the ordering the merge uses, so a parent that relied on the merge read the rows out of order. This adds an Iceberg-backed version of the upstream regression to TestStoragePartitionedJoins in spark/v4.2, as #18294 left it untested.
The new test, testPlannedSortedMergeKeepsOrderingAfterConfigChange:

creates a table partitioned by (id, days(arrive_time), name), with one row per partition. The scan reports no ordering, so Spark derives [id, name] from the partition keys. The splits are sorted by the full key, so within id = 1 the bb split comes before the aa one.
plans ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY name) with SPJ, partitionKeyOrdering and preserveOrderingOnCoalesce on, and checks that the window's ordering comes from a k-way merge (SortedMerge) and not a sort.
turns partitionKeyOrdering off, runs the already planned Dataset, and checks that the rows of id = 1 are numbered aa = 1, bb = 2.
runs with AQE off and on, as the upstream test does.

It is added to Spark 4.2 only: Spark 4.0 and 4.1 have no GroupPartitionsExec k-way merge, which SPARK-55715 added in 4.2.
Testing:

The new test and the rest of TestStoragePartitionedJoins pass on Spark 4.2.1, the version on main.
Against Spark 4.2.1 RC2 (staging repository orgapachespark-1537, the last build without SPARK-60044), Spark plans the k-way merge but the new test fails in both AQE modes: the rows of id = 1 are numbered in split order (expected: "aa" but was: "bb").
On Spark 4.2.0, Spark doesn't plan a k-way merge for this Iceberg scan at all and adds a Sort instead, with vectorized and row-based reads, so the bug can't be reached there and the test fails at its plan check.
spotlessCheck passes.
title: Spark 4.2: Test that a planned sorted merge keeps its ordering

The Spark ExpireSnapshots action computes expired files through the all_manifests metadata table, which is not supported for v4 tables. Guard ExpireSnapshotsSparkAction.expireFiles() to reject v4 before the expiration commit so the table is never partially mutated, reading refreshed metadata so a stale handle cannot slip an already-upgraded v4 table through.
Only this Spark action is guarded; core and other-engine expiration stay reachable on v4 (they read manifests directly, not metadata tables). The guard is also best-effort against a concurrent v3 to v4 upgrade committed between the check and RemoveSnapshots' own refresh; closing that race atomically would need a core-level gate.
Retarget TestExpireSnapshotsAction to v2/v3, gate the expire-using TestRewriteTablePaths tests to v2/v3 while keeping v4 coverage for the rest, and add TestExpireSnapshotsActionV4 for the v4 ehavior.
title: Spark: Reject ExpireSnapshots action on v4 tables

body:
Backport referenced-by from Spark 4.2. With
spark.sql.iceberg.referenced-by.enabled, tables and views read through an Iceberg view are loaded with a LoadContext carrying the referencing view chain, so REST catalogs can send referenced-by. Spark 4.1 keeps the chain when tables are reloaded before execution.
Spark before 4.2 has no relation catalog API, so Iceberg's ResolveViews expands views itself. It now expands them like Spark's own views: the view body is parsed and analyzed with the SQL configs captured at creation, columns bind by the stored query column names, and nested views fail at spark.sql.view.maxNestedViewDepth instead of overflowing the stack. CREATE VIEW captures SQL configs with the keys Spark 4.2 uses, and Spark 4.0 and 4.1 reject schema modes Iceberg views cannot honor.

RESTSessionCatalog kept requesting pages until the server returned a null next-page-token. A server that sends back a token the client has already used, such as one that repeats or alternates tokens, caused listTables, listNamespaces and listViews to loop forever, sending unlimited requests and piling up duplicate results in memory.
Each listing now tracks the page tokens it has used and fails with a RESTException when one comes back. Returning a partial listing instead would let callers mistake it for a complete result.
Fixes #17755

body:
RESTSessionCatalog serves many engine sessions, but a table FileIO cannot authenticate its catalog requests, such as credential refresh and remote signing, as the session that loaded the table. With rest.auth.file-io-session.enabled, the catalog attaches a KeyedTokenAuthSession to each table FileIO whose session differs from the catalog session. Only the key is serialized. On the loading node the session reads the current token from the AuthManager through TokenSource. On workers it resolves the key through a TokenResolver that the engine installs, and never acquires a token. Legacy OAuth2Manager sessions implement TokenSource. The catalog marks the FileIO properties so that AuthManagers refuses to build a manager from them. No FileIO consumes the session yet; S3FileIO, GCSFileIO and ADLSFileIO follow separately.
Design: https://s.apache.org/user-auth-session-in-file-io
Test plan:

Keys are shared within a session and distinct across sessions, catalog instances and server-issued table tokens, so one user's FileIO never presents another user's token.
Server config can neither enable the feature nor clear the marker, because only client properties may opt in.
Java, Kryo and FileIOParser serialization carry only the key, and ResolvingFileIO forwards the session to its delegates.
Scheduled renewal keeps each user's token for that user, and a rejected renewal fails only that user.
Every gap fails closed: no resolver, an unknown or expired key, a closed catalog, a non-bearer session, a FileIO without the mixin, a shared FileIO taking a second session, and an AuthManager loaded from marked properties.

body:
Closes #19014
InclusiveMetricsEvaluator, InclusiveStatsEvaluator, ManifestEvaluator and ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter compare an IN predicate's literals against lower and upper bounds with a linear scan, and skip the check entirely above 200 literals (#1588). Above the limit, every file, manifest or row group is kept, even when none of its bounds contain a literal.
Change

New package-private SortedInLiterals in org.apache.iceberg.expressions, used by InclusiveEvalVisitor (and so by InclusiveMetricsEvaluator and InclusiveStatsEvaluator) and ManifestEvaluator. Each evaluator creates one instance, which sorts each IN literal set once by the term's comparator (the same comparator the bounds checks already use) and caches it by the identity of the bound predicate's literal set. anyInRange(sorted, comparator, lower, upper) finds the first literal not below lower with Collections.binarySearch and checks it against upper.
ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter is in another module, so it has its own private copy of the sort cache and binary search (about 20 lines) instead of depending on a shared class.
InclusiveEvalVisitor.in(), ManifestEvaluator.in() and ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter.in() no longer have a literal limit. Every other check in those methods (nulls, NaN, unreliable bounds, nested and variant columns) is unchanged and still runs before the range check.
Sorting happens on first use, at the point where the comparator was already requested, so types without a comparator behave exactly as before.
The cache is a synchronized identity map, so an evaluator stays safe to share across threads.

Each literal set is sorted once per evaluator instance, at O(n log n). ManifestGroup caches ManifestEvaluator per spec, so that sort happens once per spec per scan. InclusiveMetricsEvaluator is built per ManifestReader, so its sort happens once per manifest opened, and the benchmark below includes that cost because it opens a new reader per op. ParquetMetricsRowGroupFilter is built per data file in ReadConf, so on executors the sort happens once per file and each row group then costs O(log n). For lists that previously exceeded the limit, this is new work per file (for 5,000 literals, on the order of 60,000 comparisons) in exchange for evaluating the row groups instead of reading them all.
The sorting is an implementation detail: this change adds no public API.
Results are unchanged: a file, manifest or row group is pruned only when no literal is within its bounds, which is the same test as before. The only behavioral change is that lists over 200 values are now evaluated.
Validation

./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-api:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.expressions.TestInclusiveMetricsEvaluator --tests org.apache.iceberg.expressions.TestInclusiveManifestEvaluator --tests org.apache.iceberg.expressions.TestEvaluator
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-core:test --tests 'org.apache.iceberg.expressions.TestInclusiveMetricsEvaluatorWith*' --tests 'org.apache.iceberg.TestInclusiveStatsEvaluator*'
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-parquet:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.parquet.TestParquet :iceberg-data:test --tests org.apache.iceberg.data.TestMetricsRowGroupFilter
./gradlew --no-daemon :iceberg-api:revapi :iceberg-parquet:revapi :iceberg-api:javadoc :iceberg-parquet:javadoc :iceberg-api:checkstyleMain :iceberg-parquet:checkstyleMain plus Spotless

Four existing assertions expected a 400-literal IN below the file's lower bound to be read because of the limit (three evaluator tests and testInLimitParquet, renamed testLargeInParquet); they now expect the file or row group to be skipped. New cases cover large lists that contain the lower bound, contain the upper bound, or fall on both sides of the bounds, for the metrics, stats, manifest and Parquet row-group evaluators.
With the 200-literal limit restored inside both binary-search helpers, every new and updated large-list assertion fails (8 tests across the metrics, stats, manifest and row-group test classes).
Planning […]
title: API, Core, Parquet: Evaluate IN predicates with binary search and remove the 200-literal limit

body:
Closes #18953.
Regression tests for SPARK-60403 (apache/spark#59653), fixed in Spark 4.2.1. Whole-stage codegen of a full outer SortMergeJoinExec, a full or build-side outer ShuffledHashJoinExec and MergeRowsExec called its functions by their bare names. Once the generated class grows past 1,000,000 characters, addNewFunction places these functions into a nested class, so the calls failed to compile and Spark silently fell back from whole-stage codegen.
Changes:

TestBase.assertCallsThroughNestedClasses: asserts that every whole-stage codegen stage of a plan compiles and that the given functions are called through a nested class instance.
TestOuterJoinCodegen: full outer sort merge join, full outer shuffled hash join and a left outer shuffled hash join that builds its hash table from the left side, over two Iceberg tables with a 5000-field struct.
TestMerge.testMergeWithWideStructCallsFunctionsThroughNestedClasses: MERGE with matched, not matched and not matched by source clauses (a full outer join) into a table with a 1000-field struct, for copy-on-write and merge-on-read.

Notes for review:

The upstream test puts a sliding-window aggregation above the join. In that layout the unfixed code still compiles, because the join's functions land in the same nested class as their caller (doAggregateWithKeys); the upstream test catches the regression by checking the call names. Writing a wide struct with no aggregation above the join keeps the calls in processNext of the outer class, where the unfixed code fails to compile.
Whole-stage codegen skips plans with more fields than spark.sql.codegen.maxFields (100 by default, nested fields included), so the tests raise that limit. They also disable spark.sql.codegen.fallback, so a compile error fails the test instead of falling back.
The struct widths (5000 for the joins, 1000 for MERGE) depend on how much code Spark generates. 2500 and 500 were not enough, so a future Spark version may need different values.
The MERGE test runs only for the Parquet parameters, since the generated code doesn't depend on the file format.

Testing:

Passes on Spark 4.2.1 (TestOuterJoinCodegen ~24 s; MERGE ~9 s copy-on-write, ~3 s merge-on-read).
With spark42 = "4.2.0" the new tests fail with "A method named ... is not declared in any enclosing class".

Co-Authored with Claude Opus 5.5. I reviewed the code and ran the tests locally.
cc @manuzhang
title: Spark 4.2: Test outer joins and MERGE with codegen functions in nested classes

body:
Closes #19026.
RewriteManifests.deleteManifest checks that each explicitly deleted manifest is still in the current snapshot, but ManifestFile equality only compares paths. When a transaction stages an append and then replaces the staged manifest in a later RewriteManifests, a concurrent commit makes the transaction retry. The staged manifest keeps its path but inherits a new sequence number and first row ID from the new manifest list, so the check passes. The caller's replacement, written from the entries of the first attempt, is then committed with the old data sequence number (format v2) or with row IDs that overlap the concurrent commit (v3 and v4).
This follows apache/iceberg-cpp#1104: validateDeletedManifests now also compares the sequence number, min sequence number and first row ID of each deleted manifest with the current manifest at the same path, and fails with a ValidationException if any of them changed. Committed manifests don't change these values, so only a manifest staged earlier in a retried transaction is rejected. The existing "could not be found" check and message are unchanged.
requiresRewrite had the same issue: a clusterBy rewrite of a staged manifest matched the manifests it rewrote in the first attempt by path, so a retry kept the manifests written from the first attempt. It now compares the same inherited metadata and performs a full rewrite if any of it changed, which reads the manifest again instead of failing.
The regression test replaceStagedManifestAfterTransactionRetry is from manuzhang#214 by @manuzhang, changed to expect the validation failure and to check that the table keeps the concurrent commit. Replacing an already committed manifest after a retry is covered by the existing testManifestReplacementConcurrentAppend. rewriteStagedManifestAfterTransactionRetry checks that a clusterBy rewrite of a staged manifest in a transaction that retries keeps the data sequence number and first row ID of the retry.
Testing:

TestRewriteManifests passes (128 tests, 9 skipped). Without the change in BaseRewriteManifests, replaceStagedManifestAfterTransactionRetry and rewriteStagedManifestAfterTransactionRetry fail for format versions 2, 3 and 4, and the rest of the suite passes.
TestTransaction (116 tests, 7 skipped) and TestRowLineageMetadata (21 tests) pass.
spotlessCheck passes.
title: Core: Reject a replaced manifest whose inherited metadata changed on retry

This is a minimal set of changes to get v4 writes working with SnapshotProducer and MergingSnapshotProducer. Root manifests are managed and written by RootManifestProducer, which is roughly the v4 equivalent of MergingSnapshotProducer. Initially, I thought that it would be easier to replace MergingSnapshotProducer with a v4 version, but in the end that strategy would require a lot of churn with little benefit, so I decided to add a delegate within the class instead. Why
RewriteTablePath lists the statistics and partition statistics files of every version file it stages. An incremental copy therefore lists the start version's statistics files again, although an earlier copy moved them and the docs say it returns only files added in the range. How
This change lists only the end version's statistics files that the start version does not hold, which includes new ones for existing snapshots. Files referenced only by older versions are no longer listed, matching manifest lists.

body:
Closes #19047
Background
When a manifest list (or any other file) is deleted from GCS but still referenced by metadata, reading it fails with an NPE instead of a NotFoundException:
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "com.google.cloud.storage.Blob.getSize()" because the return value of "org.apache.iceberg.gcp.gcs.GCSInputFile.getBlob()" is null
	at org.apache.iceberg.gcp.gcs.GCSInputFile.getLength(GCSInputFile.java:59)
	at org.apache.iceberg.avro.AvroIterable.newFileReader(AvroIterable.java:102)

Root cause
Storage.get(BlobId) returns null for a missing object (that's also what BaseGCSFile.exists() relies on). GCSInputFile.getLength() called getBlob().getSize() without a null check. #15734 already maps 404s to NotFoundException in the input streams, but getLength() runs before any stream is opened (e.g. AvroIterable.newFileReader), so the NPE comes first.
Fix
If the blob is missing, getLength() throws NotFoundException("Location does not exist: %s", location()), the same message GCSExceptionUtil and S3InputStream use. Nothing else changes: a known length still skips the lookup.
Tests

New TestGcsInputFile#getLengthMissingBlob: storage.get returns null, exists() is false and getLength() throws NotFoundException with the location.
./gradlew :iceberg-gcp:test and :iceberg-gcp:spotlessCheck pass locally (JDK 21). I didn't run the GCS integration tests (gcp/src/integration), they need the emulator.

Limitations

Only the getLength() path is covered here. Other callers of getBlob() (exists()) already handle null.
#16935 tried to improve the error for a missing manifest list at the core level and was closed as stale; this one fixes it where the NPE happens instead.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) to help write this change and the test. I reviewed the code and ran the tests myself.
Happy to adjust anything, e.g. the message wording or moving the check into BaseGCSFile, lmk.

body:
DynamicWriter and DynamicWriteResultAggregator cache a RowDataTaskWriterFactory / ManifestOutputFileFactory per table, and each captures the Table returned by catalog.loadTable(...). That Table holds the full TableMetadata, including every snapshot and its summary, for as long as the entry stays in the cache. Neither factory needs snapshots: the writer uses the table's IO, location provider, encryption, schema, spec and properties, and the manifest factory uses the IO and the metadata directory.
With many tables and long snapshot histories this dominates the TaskManager heap. In our deployment (about 1,400 tables, the largest with ~33k unexpired snapshots, roughly 9 GB of metadata.json in total), a class histogram showed ~16-18M BaseSnapshot objects plus their summary maps and strings, more than 40 GB of heap. That is about twice the snapshot count on disk, since each table is loaded once by the writer and once by the aggregator.
This change:

DynamicWriter: the cached writer factory gets SerializableTable.copyOf(table), as FlinkSink and IcebergSink already do for their writers.
DynamicWriteResultAggregator: resolves the table's metadata directory once while the loaded table is available, passes it through flink.manifests.location (unless the user already set it), and gives the cached manifest factory a SerializableTable.
ManifestOutputFileFactory: only calls operations() when no manifest location is configured. On a SerializableTable, operations() reloads the full metadata and its metadataFileLocation(...) throws, so the call has to be skipped when it is not needed. FLINK_MANIFEST_LOCATION becomes public so the dynamic sink can use it.

Manifest paths are unchanged; the new aggregator test asserts the path equals the table's own metadataFileLocation(name).
Open points for reviewers:

The metadata directory is derived from metadataFileLocation("probe") minus the file name, because HadoopTableOperations rejects an empty file name. An alternative is a FlinkManifestUtil.createOutputFileFactory overload that takes the directory directly instead of reusing the flink.manifests.location property. Happy to switch if that is preferred.
This PR only changes Flink 2.3. I can backport it to 2.2 and 1.20 here or in a follow-up PR.

Testing: added TestDynamicWriter#testCachedWriterFactoryDoesNotRetainTableMetadata and TestDynamicWriteResultAggregator#testCachedOutputFileFactoryDoesNotRetainTableMetadata; both fail without the change. Ran the iceberg-flink-2.3 module tests and spotlessCheck.
AI disclosure: I used Claude Code (an AI coding assistant) to help analyze the heap issue, trace the retention through the sink code, and draft the change and tests. I reviewed the code and ran the tests myself.
title: Flink: Avoid retaining full table metadata in DynamicSink writer and aggregator caches

body:
ConvertEqualityDeletes keeps every live row of the target branch in its PK index, so state grows with the table even when updates reach only recent partitions. This PR adds partitionIndexIdleTimeout (off by default): the planner indexes a partition when its first equality delete arrives and evicts it after the timeout passes without one. An unpartitioned delete indexes every partition. A partition that receives rows in the evicting cycle is kept, because the worker could apply those rows after the eviction. Changing the setting rebuilds the index on restore.
Open question: lazy loading without eviction never indexes or reads more than the full index, at the cost of planning the snapshot when deletes first reach a partition. Should it become the only mode, with the idle timeout controlling only eviction?
Tests:

Planner:

a partition is loaded on its first delete (every partition for an unpartitioned delete) and not again while it stays indexed
each delete restarts the timeout of the partitions it applies to, and a partition is evicted once its timeout passes, unless the cycle sends rows to it
after an eviction or a rebuild, the next delete that reaches a partition loads it again
staging and external files of unindexed partitions are skipped
on restore, the index is rebuilt when the index mode changes

Worker: eviction removes only the evicted partitions' rows and leaves no state for emptied keys.
End to end: a partition evicted and reloaded with earlier DVs gives correct results.

Closes #19040.
This removes -NaN from the float sort order and states that all NaN bit patterns compare equal, which is what Float.compare and Double.compare do and what the sentence after the order already claims. The rule constrains comparison only, so writers don't canonicalize the NaN values they store. It matches how the spec already treats NaN elsewhere: expression equality, partition value equality, and bucket hashing all treat every NaN bit pattern as one value.
@pvary suggested keeping the order and removing the Java claim. This PR changes the order to match Java instead, for the reasons in this reply.
This is a spec-only change. Iceberg Java already sorts this way through Comparator.naturalOrder().

This is a git revert of ea47af3 from #18394 with one manual conflict resolution in TestV4ManifestReader. #18598 later removed the false tight-stats argument from the new FieldStatsStruct<>(...) call in the geoFieldStats helper that #18394 added. The whole helper is removed in the revert.
#18394 reads geo bounds as GeospatialBound. Readers fill custom structs by position, so projecting a subset of the coordinates, for example only lower_bound.m, stored M as X (discussion). #18394 worked around this by always projecting the full geo bound struct, which reads columns the caller didn't request. @rdblue recommended offline that Iceberg shouldn't project additional data like the entire bound.
The spec says that if either the X or Y dimension is missing, the bounding box is not produced. GeospatialBound represents a bounding-box corner and should guarantee valid X and Y, so it shouldn't represent a partially projected bound. Making it projection-aware would also add a mutable StructLike with stats schema knowledge to the api module.
After this revert:

Write path: unchanged. GeospatialBound keeps the read-only StructLike the writer uses.
Read path: back to the generic struct, which supports any projection, including m-only, without reading extra columns. A custom core struct for reads didn't seem worth it compared with the generic struct.

The trade-off is that the two paths aren't symmetric: writes take a GeospatialBound, and reads return a generic struct.

#19050 changes it to look fields up by name and treats a bound without X or Y as no bound.

Bumps datamodel-code-generator from 0.91.0 to 0.96.0.

Release notes
Sourced from datamodel-code-generator's releases.

0.96.0
Breaking Changes
Code Generation Changes

Generated client methods return raw bodies for itemSchema stream responses - For an OpenAPI 3.2 response media of text/event-stream or a JSON Lines or NDJSON type (application/jsonl, application/jsonlines, application/ndjson, application/x-jsonl, application/x-jsonlines, application/x-ndjson) whose schema is only an itemSchema, the generated client no longer binds the model of the item schema's array projection to the operation's response. The operation method, its with_response view and its result type alias now read the whole body raw: str for an event stream (a text branch) and bytes for JSON Lines or NDJSON (a binary branch). For example, WatchEventsResponse becomes str, and a JSON plus JSON Lines response becomes models.ExcerptGetResponse | bytes. Code that relied on the old result type must parse the raw body or use the new stream helper that regenerated clients now get at client.protocols.<resource>.<method>, which yields typed items (#6767)
Generated client stream helpers now type items as the model the itemSchema references - In generated Python clients, SSE, JSON Lines and NDJSON stream helpers whose itemSchema is a bare $ref now use the referenced model, for example EventStream[models.LogEntry], AsyncEventStream[models.Event] and EventPlan[models.LogEntry]. Before, they used the duplicate ItemSchema or ItemSchemaModel model generated at the item schema location. The codecs in _generated/model_bindings.py change to match. With Pydantic v2 output, decoded stream items are now instances of the referenced model, for example models.LogEntry instead of models.ItemSchemaModel, and validation error messages name that model. With dataclasses output, only the type annotations change. Code that annotates, isinstance-checks or pattern-matches stream items against models.ItemSchema or models.ItemSchemaModel has to switch to the referenced model (#6771)
Const, enum and allOf branches no longer take object keywords under --read-object-keywords-by-type - With --read-object-keywords-by-type, which the standard and practical 20261112 presets also turn on, the check for an anyOf or oneOf branch that admits no object now looks at more than a declared type or a $ref to such a schema. It also counts const, enum, nested allOf, anyOf and oneOf parts, false schemas, and the full schema a $ref names together with the keywords beside it. Branches found this way are now read without the sibling properties, patternProperties, additionalProperties, propertyNames, unevaluatedProperties, required, minProperties and maxProperties. For example, an anyOf of a const branch, an enum branch and an object branch next to properties and required used to generate a single model field Owner | None and now generates a union like Literal['none'] | Owner | Owner1 | None. That adds new enum classes and can shift model names: the former Owner model becomes Owner1. Under --generate-schema-validators these sites also become unions instead of one validated object model. Output without the option is unchanged (#6777)
Regex patterns containing quotes are written differently in Pydantic v2 output - With pydantic_v2.BaseModel and pydantic_v2.dataclass output, a pattern containing a single quote used to be written as a single-quoted raw literal with the quote escaped by a backslash, for example constr(pattern=r'^it\'s$'). Because raw literals keep backslashes, the runtime pattern string had an extra backslash before the quote. The generator now picks a quote character the pattern does not use, so this becomes constr(pattern=r"^it's$"). A pattern containing both quote characters is now written as a plain (non-raw) literal, for example '^a-z\'"+$' instead of r'^a-z\'"+$', and backslashes in such patterns are doubled. A pattern that already holds a backslash before a quote changes only in source text: "^don\ […]

Release notes
Sourced from actions/setup-java's releases.

v6.3.0
Behavior change: Java problem matcher is now opt-in
Starting with v6.3.0, setup-java no longer registers the Java problem matcher by default (#1326, fixes #1322). Java compiler warnings, compiler errors, and uncaught exceptions are no longer turned into annotations on pull request diffs unless you opt in.
To keep annotations, set problem-matcher: true:
- uses: actions/setup-java@v6
  with:
    distribution: temurin
    java-version: '25'
    problem-matcher: true
Compiler output still appears in the build logs, and compilation errors still fail the build. Only annotations are affected.
Why: inline annotations cluttered pull request reviews, and GitHub Actions caps annotations at 10 errors, 10 warnings, and 10 notices per step, and 50 per job. Larger Java builds therefore showed only a truncated subset of their diagnostics as annotations. See Java problem matcher (compiler annotations).

Bumps bouncycastle from 1.86 to 1.87.
Updates org.bouncycastle:bcpkix-jdk18on from 1.86 to 1.87

Changelog
Sourced from org.bouncycastle:bcpkix-jdk18on's changelog.

Version 1.87
Release: 1.87
Date: 2026, 11th November.
Defects Fixed

PrivateKeyFactory, and so the ML-DSA and ML-KEM KeyFactory services, ignored the tag of the RFC 9881 / RFC 9935 private key CHOICE and applied no length checks, so mislabelled or inconsistent seed, expandedKey and both forms were accepted. Each form is now checked for its tag, exact lengths and consistency; the pre-RFC draft forms are still read.
X500Name.equals was quadratic in the number of RDNs for names that are equal but not byte-identical, and is reached from unverified CMS, TSP and S/MIME messages; the CMS signer and recipient stores could also be slowed with colliding ids. Name comparison is now n log n and the stores no longer hash their entries (CVE-2026-103611).
Tables keyed on ASN.1 object hash codes, which a sender can make collide - Extensions, X509Extensions, ExtendedKeyUsage, the CMS AttributeTable, the EST CSRAttributesResponse and the CMS digest algorithm sets - made parsing quadratic in the number of entries. They are now ordered maps and sets.
CMSSignedData digested the content once for every signer verified. Signers using the same digest algorithm now share one digest, and the new org.bouncycastle.cms.max_digest_algorithms property can bound the number of distinct digest algorithms computed over one message.
The verify side of the ML-DSA-CALCULATE-MU signature service, and MLDSASigner.verifyMu, did not absorb the message, so a correct mu was accepted only for an empty message, and the signer was left unusable afterwards. verifyMu now derives mu as generateMu does and compares in constant time.
KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("SM2", "BC") was built on the generic EC generator and could draw a private key of n - 1, which GB/T 32918.1 excludes. It now uses SM2KeyPairGenerator.
ESTResponse was quadratic in the number of repeated header lines, and a read limit only applied after the header block. Header values are now collected once and the header block counts against the read limit.
The C509 encoding of RFC 6955 proof-of-possession signature values and of the RFC 9883 privateKeyPossessionStatement attribute did not follow draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert-21 and could not be reconstructed. Both now convert in each direction, and the draft-ietf-cose-c509-test-vectors-02 vectors drive the tests.
DANE SMIMEA support: JndiDANEFetcherFactory mangled the owner name of listed records so lookups failed, DANEEntryStore kept only one entry per owner name, and DANEEntrySelectorFactory mishandled addresses with a quoted local-part or no '@'. All three are corrected, and DANEEntry rejects a record that is not a full certificate entry.
TimeStampToken accepted a token whose signing-time attribute disagreed with the genTime in its TSTInfo. Such a token is now rejected (org.bouncycastle.tsp.allow_inconsistent_signing_time switches the check off), and TimeStampTokenGenerator sets signing-time from the genTime (CVE-2026-103615).
TimeStampToken.validate() accepted an MD5 message imprint and TSPAlgorithms.ALLOWED included MD5. MD5 is removed from ALLOWED, validate() rejects an imprint algorithm outside the allowed set, and TSPAlgorithms.LEGACY and org.bouncycastle.tsp.allowed_imprint_algorithms are provided for callers needing it (CVE-2026-103606).
CRL-based revocation checking mishandled a CRL entry reasonCode outside the RFC 5280 set: 11 left the certificate unrevoked and other values threw an unchecked exception. An undefined reasonCode is now processed as unspecified.
OERDefinition.enumItem(label, value) discarded the explicit enumerand value. The value is now kept and unnumbered items are numbered as X.680 sec. 20 specifies.
OERInputStream did not detect a stream ending inside an INTEGER or BIT STRING value, decoding the zero-padded buffer instead. Length-driven reads now fail with EOFException and […]

body:
Summary
Fixes #19087
This PR fixes a Flink SQL filter pushdown issue where comparisons between FLOAT/DOUBLE columns and DECIMAL literals can fail during Iceberg predicate binding.
For example:
SELECT id, score
FROM t_double
WHERE score <= 14.3;
Flink represents the DECIMAL literal as java.math.BigDecimal. When this value is pushed into an Iceberg predicate against a DOUBLE column, predicate binding can throw:
ValidationException: Invalid value for conversion to type double: 14.3 (java.math.BigDecimal)

Root Cause
FlinkFilters.convertFieldAndLiteral() converts Flink DECIMAL literals into BigDecimal values without checking whether the target Iceberg column supports that literal type.
This can create incompatible Iceberg predicates that fail during manifest evaluation.
Solution
This PR introduces a conservative correctness fix:

Detect BigDecimal literals compared against FLOAT or DOUBLE fields.
Decline unsafe predicate pushdown by returning Optional.empty().
Handle both field–literal and literal–field comparison directions.
Preserve valid DECIMAL-column predicate pushdown.
Apply the fix consistently across Flink 1.20, 2.2, and 2.3.

The affected predicates remain available for evaluation by Flink rather than being pushed into Iceberg.
Regression Tests
Added tests covering:

FLOAT and DOUBLE comparisons with DECIMAL literals.
Both comparison directions.
Mixed predicates containing supported and unsupported filters.
Existing DECIMAL-column predicate compatibility.
End-to-end Flink 2.3 SQL execution against a nonempty Iceberg table.

The SQL integration test verifies that WHERE score <= 14.3 executes successfully and returns the expected rows.
Validation

Flink 1.20 TestFlinkFilters — Passed
Flink 2.2 TestFlinkFilters — Passed
Flink 2.3 TestFlinkFilters — Passed
Flink 2.3 SQL integration regression test — Passed
Spotless Java checks across all three versions — Passed
Git whitespace validation — Passed

Design Consideration
This approach prioritizes correctness over filter pushdown for mixed DECIMAL/floating-point comparisons.
It avoids potentially unsafe numeric coercion and preserves SQL evaluation through Flink. Maintainer feedback on the approach is welcome.
title: Flink: Avoid unsafe decimal literal pushdown to floating-point fields

body:
Once a branch and main point to different snapshots, IcebergSource streaming from the branch starts from main's snapshot. The symptoms depend on starting-strategy:

INCREMENTAL_FROM_LATEST_SNAPSHOT (default) and INCREMENTAL_FROM_LATEST_SNAPSHOT_EXCLUSIVE: silently re-emit branch commits from before the start point.
INCREMENTAL_FROM_SNAPSHOT_TIMESTAMP: fails to start, or re-emits older commits once main moves.
INCREMENTAL_FROM_EARLIEST_SNAPSHOT: fails with an ancestry error once main's older snapshots are expired.
TABLE_SCAN_THEN_INCREMENTAL, once main has a newer commit: emits rows not in the branch and skips the branch's own rows. If a checkpoint completes first, those rows can reach the sink, and restoring that position fails ancestry validation on every restart, with an error that never mentions the bad rows.

This change resolves automatically selected starting snapshots and timestamp-based starting snapshots from the configured branch, and fails fast when the branch does not exist (previously it idled, or read main). The jobs already restored from an affected checkpoint must restart without state.
Repro: create branch b1 and commit to it, then stream b1 with the default starting strategy. Before: the existing b1 commits are emitted again. After: only the branch's latest snapshot and later commits.
Test plan: four TestContinuousSplitPlannerImpl tests (latest-exclusive, timestamp, earliest after main expiration, missing branch), each failing on main and passing with the fix.
title: Flink: Fix silent duplicate rows or rows not in the branch when streaming from a branch

body:
Follow up PR for #14590. From #14590, #18377 was created to fix part of the problem that is leaking closed Spark sessions. However, with Iceberg 1.12, each RESTSessionCatalog creates its own rest-metrics-reporter executor (#16695). Those threads lives until catalog is closed. In this case, when the compute engine (e.g. Spark Connect) don't close catalogs during Spark Connection idle session releases, those ended up keep one thread per catalog.
This PR makes the metrics executor's thread exit after 60s idle and not inherit thread-locals or the context class loader. The executor itself is created inside the RESTSessionCatalog.
title: Core: exit idle REST metrics reporter threads

CatalogHandlers.planTableScan treated min-rows-requested as a cap on the number of file scan tasks, assuming each task yields at least one row. A task whose rows are removed by delete files or by its residual filter can yield none, so the server could return fewer rows than the scan contains; with Spark's LIMIT pushdown against a REST table using server-side planning, LIMIT 1 could return no rows. Planning now stops only once tasks without delete files and with an always-true residual cover the requested rows, the same rule #18715 uses for local planning.

Files with a non-trivial residual do not count toward the requested rows, for both planning modes.
The existing scanPlanningWithMinRowsRequested still returns a single task when files have no deletes and no residual.

body:
Data manifests written by v1/v2 tables have no first_row_id. When such a table is upgraded directly to v4, these manifests are carried into the root as EXISTING entries and should be assigned a first_row_id.
The root manifest writer already assigns it and counts the rows, but RootTrackedFileWrapper rejects the assignment with "Missing first-row-id for EXISTING file", so the first append after the upgrade fails. This fixes RootTrackedFileWrapper to allow the assignment for EXISTING data manifests without a first_row_id; other entries without one are still rejected.
Test plan:

v1/v2 table with a snapshot, upgrade to v4, append: the root holds the new file (ADDED) and the carried-forward manifest (EXISTING) with assigned the first_row_id.
Root wrapper assigns first_row_id to an EXISTING data manifest without one.
Root wrapper still rejects DELETED, REPLACED, and MODIFIED entries without first_row_id.

Generated-by: Cursor (Claude Opus 5.5)
title: Core: Assign first-row-id to pre-v3 manifests carried into v4 root

body:
Flink compares a column with a wider numeric literal in the wider type, but FlinkFilters pushed the literal down unchanged and binding converted it to the column type. This narrowed values (f > 0.1E0 on a FLOAT column dropped matching rows, as did a DOUBLE literal on a DECIMAL column) or threw ValidationException (i > 6.5, i > 6.0, d > 0.1 on a DOUBLE column). This converts the literal by value and pushes the comparison down only when the column type represents it exactly, otherwise leaving the filter to Flink. Compared with #19103, which skips pushdown whenever the types differ, this keeps pushdown for literals such as d > 0, f > 0.5E0, i > 6.0 and d > 0.1.
Fixes #19102
Test plan: TestFlinkFilters checks that exact literals are pushed with the converted value and inexact ones are not, for each numeric column type and with the literal on either side. TestFlinkTableSource checks query results and the pushed filter for an INT, a DOUBLE and a FLOAT column.
title: Flink: Push down numeric comparisons only when the literal is exact in the column type

body:
Fixes #19110.
pushPredicates drops a predicate from the post-scan filters when it selects whole partitions. Iceberg expressions are two-valued, so for a NULL partition value notEq, notIn, notStartsWith and notNaN are true, while SQL treats them as unknown. Spark adds IS NOT NULL for a top-level comparison, which hides this, but under OR or NOT the NULL partition is selected and nothing filters it out.
The predicate is now evaluated completely by Iceberg only if, after rewriteNot, every leaf gives the SQL result for NULL (=, IN, STARTS_WITH, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, isNaN) or is on a column that a top-level or sibling IS NOT NULL keeps non-null. Everything else stays a post-scan filter. Plans for top-level comparisons, NOT IN and IS NULL are unchanged, so aggregate pushdown is not affected for them.
This is the scan side of #18605; #18617 changes the DELETE conversion and leaves scans as they are. Backports to the other Spark versions can follow.
Testing: testFilterPushdownWithNegatedPredicatesOnNullPartition in TestFilterPushDown, which fails without the change, and the existing TestFilterPushDown and TestAggregatePushDown suites. I also ran the queries from the issue against a runtime jar built from this branch on Spark 4.2.1.
AI tools helped draft the change and tests; I reviewed and tested them.
title: Spark 4.2: Keep post-scan filter for partition predicates that are not NULL-safe

Summary
CatalogUtil.loadFileIO creates a FileIO, applies Hadoop configuration and storage credentials, and calls initialize. If any of these steps throws a Exception, the instance is never returned to the caller and any resources acquired during construction or setup leak.
This change closes the FileIO instance when setup fails and rethrows the original exception, attaching any failure from close() as suppressed via Exceptions.suppressExceptions. Successful loads remain unchanged.
Test Plan

Parameterized failure tests across configuration, credentials, and initialize verifying fileIO.close() is called once and the original exception is rethrown.
Suppressed exception handling when close() also throws during failure cleanup.
Successful initialization returning an open FileIO instance.

body:
Closes #19109
Projected scans were reporting schemaId = 0 because TypeUtil.project builds a new schema with the default id, and SnapshotScan.planFiles used schema().schemaId() (the projected schema) in the report.
The report already carries projected_field_ids / projected_field_names, so I just switched that to tableSchema().schemaId() — the schema the projection comes from. For data scans, useSnapshot() already replaces tableSchema() with the snapshot schema, so time travel stays correct. Left TypeUtil.project alone. Incremental / changelog scans don't emit ScanReports, so no change there.
Tests in ScanPlanningAndReportingTestBase (format v2/v3): evolve the schema first so the id isn't 0, then assert a projected select report uses the table schema id; plus a time-travel case that lands on an older evolved snapshot and checks that snapshot's id.

body:
Follow-up to #17622, as discussed in #17622 (comment).
RepairTable commits its repaired manifests with RewriteManifests, and a REPLACE snapshot keeps the parent snapshot's totals. So after a repair, total-records, total-files-size, total-position-deletes and total-equality-deletes still reflect the incorrect stats.
This adds RewriteManifests.adjustTotal(String totalProperty, long delta). The caller passes how much a total changes, and core adds that to the totals of the snapshot the commit lands on, so the totals stay correct when the commit is retried on a newer snapshot. Only the record count and file size totals can be adjusted, since the replaced and new manifests must hold the same files.
RepairTable on Spark 4.2 now works out the deltas while it checks each entry: the record count and file size it will write, minus the stored ones. It sums them per total and passes them to adjustTotal. I'll backport the Spark change to 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 once this lands.
Tests:

TestRewriteManifests: deltas for two corrected files, one of them negative, are summed into the totals, and they are applied to the latest snapshot when the commit lands after a concurrent append. File count totals are rejected.
TestRepairTableAction: after repairing a data file, an equality delete, a position delete, and a manifest that holds both delete types, the snapshot totals match the repaired files.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.
title: Core, Spark 4.2: Correct snapshot totals when RepairTable repairs stats

body:
Part of #18142
Previously, the lookup join full cache was rebuilt from scratch on every reload, even when only new rows were added.
This change enables incremental cache updates by reading only newly added rows and merging them into the existing cache.
Incremental updates are supported only when all snapshots are Append or Replace (e.g., compaction). Otherwise, or if the incremental read fails, it falls back to a full cache rebuild.
title: Flink: Lookup join cache support incremental reload via snapshot deltas
